title: Periodic Inspection and Testing (Condition Reporting)
subtitle: Five Periodic Inspection and Condition Reporting practice tests
description: A merged advanced exam for periodic inspection, testing and condition reporting. It combines the periodic inspection bank with the EICR coding and reporting bank so each attempt tests both the inspection process and the final condition reporting judgement. Questions focus on GN3 intervals, sampling, limitations, dead/live testing, EICR documentation, C1/C2/C3/FI coding, PRS duties, duty-holder communication and defensible technical decisions.
format: Five rotating 40-question practice tests. Exam format: 60 minutes, open book (IET Guidance Note 3). Pass at 75%+.

questions.prompt: If an EICR for a rented dwelling identifies a C1 or C2 item, or requires further investigation, the landlord under the 2020 private rented sector electrical safety duties must normally arrange the required remedial or investigative work within:

options.B: Before the next EICR cycle
options.C: 28 days, or sooner if the report specifies a shorter period

questions.explanation: For rented dwellings covered by the 2020 regulations in England, remedial or further investigative work must normally be completed within 28 days, unless the report specifies a shorter period. A C1 still needs immediate safety action; the legal 28-day period is not permission to leave danger present.

questions.prompt: Periodic inspection of a school is being planned. The installation is heavily used and contains kitchens, science labs and ICT rooms. The most defensible interval choice is:

options.A: Apply the commercial/educational starting point and adjust for use, with shorter intervals or sampling for higher-risk areas
options.B: Use a 25-year interval to match the expected life of the building
options.C: Treat it as domestic and inspect every 10 years throughout
options.D: Treat the entire school as a swimming pool and inspect everything annually

questions.explanation: Inspection frequency should be risk-based. A school is not a normal dwelling, and kitchens, labs and ICT areas may justify closer attention than low-risk rooms. A single blanket interval without considering use, environment and previous condition is weak practice.

questions.prompt: A landlord asks you to "just issue a pass certificate" for a flat. You are allowed access only to the consumer unit, hallway socket and kitchen. Bedrooms, bathroom, loft and built-in appliances are inaccessible. What is the best response?

options.A: Issue a satisfactory EICR because limitations can cover anything not inspected
options.B: Refuse to issue any report under all circumstances
options.C: Issue only a report for the agreed accessible extent, clearly recording the limitations, and do not imply that the whole flat has been verified
options.D: Record every inaccessible room as C2

questions.explanation: Limitations must be agreed and recorded, but they must not be used to create a misleading "pass." If the limitations prevent a meaningful safety assessment, you should refuse to give the impression that the whole installation is satisfactory. Inaccessible areas are not automatically C2; they are limitations or not verified items unless a defect is actually identified.

questions.prompt: A new radial socket circuit was installed two weeks ago by an unknown person. No Electrical Installation Certificate is available. The client asks you to "certify it retrospectively" during an EICR. What is the correct approach?

options.A: Issue an Electrical Installation Certificate as long as the test results are satisfactory
options.B: Include the circuit within the EICR as existing work, inspect and test it as far as practicable, and avoid implying responsibility for its design and construction
options.C: Automatically code the circuit C1 because the original certificate is missing
options.D: Ignore the circuit because it is too new to inspect periodically

questions.explanation: An EICR reports on the condition of an existing installation. It is not a retrospective design-and-construction certificate for work done by someone else. Missing documentation may justify FI if safety-critical information cannot be verified, but the missing certificate alone is not automatically C1 or C2.

questions.prompt: An owner-occupied flat is up for sale. The buyer asks whether the existing 8-year-old EICR is still valid. The most accurate response is:

options.A: Yes — owner-occupied is 10 years and the report runs to that date
options.B: Yes — EICRs run for 25 years
options.C: GN3 recommends a fresh EICR at change of occupancy regardless of how recent the previous report was
options.D: No — once the property is for sale all reports are void

questions.explanation: The 10-year owner-occupied figure is qualified by 'or at change of occupancy if sooner'. A new occupier needs an up-to-date condition assessment — the previous report cannot speak to alterations or wear since it was issued.

questions.prompt: A landlord re-lets a privately rented house in England. The previous EICR is dated 4 years and 11 months ago and was satisfactory. Under ESS PRS Regs 2020 the landlord must:

options.A: Carry the existing EICR forward to the next tenant for the remaining 1 month and then re-test
options.B: Provide the existing EICR to the new tenant before they move in and arrange a fresh inspection before the 5-year date
options.C: Carry out a fresh EICR every change of tenancy
options.D: Wait until the existing report has expired

questions.explanation: ESS PRS sets a 5-year max with the EICR supplied to a new tenant before move-in. A fresh inspection is not legally required at every tenancy change — but it is best practice if the report is close to expiry.

questions.prompt: A small office unit on a business park, last EICR 5 years ago and Satisfactory. Recommended interval for the next inspection is:

options.B: 3 years

questions.explanation: Commercial premises (offices, shops, restaurants) are typically 5 years in GN3. The duty holder may shorten this if conditions, occupation, or use have changed since the last inspection.

questions.prompt: A working farm with milking parlour, grain store and farmhouse — recommended interval for the agricultural buildings:

options.B: 3 years

questions.explanation: Agricultural and horticultural premises are typically 3 years. The mix of livestock, dust, ammonia, washdown water and rough handling drives a shorter interval than commercial.

questions.prompt: A theatre stage installation: recommended IET maximum interval:

options.B: 3 years

questions.explanation: Places of public entertainment, theatres and similar are commonly given a 1-year maximum interval — public access plus heavy temporary lighting/sound use justify the shorter figure.

questions.prompt: A construction site has its temporary supply panel and 110 V transformer in continuous use. The recommended periodic inspection interval is:

options.B: 1 year

questions.explanation: Construction-site installations are typically reviewed every 3 months in GN3 because of the constant mechanical abuse, weather exposure and frequent reconfiguration of the temporary system.

questions.prompt: Marina and inland-navigation berths: recommended IET maximum interval:

options.B: 3 years

questions.explanation: Marina pedestals are 1 year. Salt or fresh water plus exposed-location plug and socket work plus constant connect/disconnect cycles add up to a high-risk LV environment.

questions.prompt: A privately rented HMO has been refurbished. The contractor wants to know whether they need an EIC, an EICR, or both:

options.A: EICR only — refurbishment is not new work
options.B: EIC for the new circuits installed during refurbishment, plus the existing EICR cycle continues for the wider installation
options.D: Neither is needed — the landlord just needs a receipt

questions.explanation: New circuits are certified by an EIC at handover. The wider installation continues to be assessed periodically by EICR. Mixing the two is a common confusion: certificates cover new work; reports cover existing in-service work.

questions.prompt: Following an electric shock incident on the premises, the recommended action regarding the periodic inspection interval is:

options.A: Wait until the next scheduled date
options.B: Trigger an unscheduled periodic inspection so the cause can be investigated and the wider installation reviewed

questions.explanation: Significant incidents (shock, fire, flood, major damage) are recognised triggers in GN3 for an out-of-cycle periodic inspection. The previous interval cannot anticipate the post-incident state of the installation.

questions.prompt: GN3 Table 3.2 intervals are best understood as:

options.A: Statutory maxima that cannot be reduced
options.B: Risk-based starting points to be adjusted by the duty holder for actual conditions, use and previous results
options.C: Suggested minima that can be lengthened freely
options.D: Targets that override the in-service safety duty between inspections

questions.explanation: GN3 intervals are starting points — the duty holder still owns in-service safety throughout. Conditions, alterations, abuse and previous EICR findings all justify shortening (or in some cases extending) the headline figure.

questions.prompt: A converted barn now used as a small commercial bakery. Previous use was domestic. The change of use means:

options.A: The previous domestic 10-year interval continues unchanged
options.B: A fresh inspection should be carried out and the future interval re-set against the new use (typically commercial 5 years)
options.C: No EICR is required because the building has not changed
options.D: The interval defaults to a 1-year cycle automatically

questions.explanation: Change of use changes the load profile, the legislative regime and the risk profile. GN3 treats this as a trigger for a fresh inspection and a re-set interval based on the new use category.

questions.prompt: BS 7671 Reg 651.1 lists the objectives of periodic inspection and testing. Which of these is NOT one of them?

options.A: Verify the safety of persons and livestock against electric shock and burns
options.B: Verify protection against damage to property by fire and heat
options.C: Verify the original installer was properly qualified and certified
options.D: Verify the installation is not damaged or defective so as to impair safety

questions.explanation: Reg 651.1 covers shock/burn safety, fire protection, freedom from damage and freedom from defects. The competence of the original installer is a wider question for the duty holder, not a Reg 651.1 objective.

questions.prompt: A privately rented dwelling has a C2 observation on its EICR. The landlord must complete remedial work within:

options.A: 28 days, or sooner if specified by the inspector
options.B: 3 months

questions.explanation: ESS PRS 2020: any C1, C2 or FI requires written confirmation that remedial work was completed within 28 days, or shorter where the inspector specifies. The remedial confirmation must go to the tenant and to the local authority on request.

questions.prompt: A church hall with infrequent occasional use — typical IET-recommended interval:

options.A: 1 year because it is public assembly
options.B: Treated as a place of public assembly, often 1-3 years depending on use, with judgement for infrequent occupation
options.D: 25 years — long life for low-use buildings

questions.explanation: Public-assembly venues sit in the 1-3 year band. The duty holder uses judgement on actual occupancy and risk — infrequent use justifies the longer end of the band, but never extends to domestic-style intervals.

questions.prompt: A holiday-let chalet that is not strictly a 'rental dwelling' under the PRS Regs. The most defensible interval position is:

options.A: Apply the GN3 interval for caravan parks/holiday units (typically 1-3 years)
options.B: Apply the owner-occupied 10-year figure
options.D: No EICR is needed because PRS Regs do not apply

questions.explanation: Holiday lets are typically inspected on the holiday-park / rental-unit cycle (1-3 years depending on the layout). The PRS Regs are residential-tenancy specific, but EAWR and GN3 apply regardless.

questions.prompt: Periodic inspection in the workplace is principally driven by which legislation?

options.B: RIDDOR 2013
options.C: The Electricity at Work Regulations 1989 (Reg 4(2)) and the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974

questions.explanation: EAWR Reg 4(2) requires that systems be maintained so as to prevent danger; HSWA places the general duty on the employer. Periodic inspection is the recognised means of demonstrating that the duty has been discharged.

questions.prompt: A small dental practice on the high street (commercial use, public access). Reasonable starting interval for the next EICR:

options.B: 3 years

questions.explanation: Commercial premises are typically 5 years. The duty holder might justify shortening (e.g. heavy use, sensitive equipment) but the GN3 starting point for general commercial is 5 years.

questions.prompt: A periodic inspection for an industrial unit reveals significant deterioration that suggests the previous interval was too long. The most defensible response for the future interval is:

options.B: Recommend a shorter interval for the next cycle and record the justification on the EICR
options.C: Recommend a longer interval to balance the books
options.D: Set the interval to 25 years to discourage retesting

questions.explanation: Findings on the current EICR feed the next interval. If deterioration is greater than expected, the duty holder shortens the interval and the inspector records the recommendation in the report.

questions.prompt: An ESS PRS Regs 2020 EICR returns Unsatisfactory because of an FI observation. The landlord's duty to act is:

options.A: Complete remedial action and obtain written confirmation within 28 days, or sooner if specified
options.B: Wait until the report expires
options.C: Ignore the FI because it is not a coded defect
options.D: Relet the property and let the new tenant decide

questions.explanation: FI also makes the report Unsatisfactory and triggers the 28-day duty under ESS PRS. The landlord must arrange the further investigation, complete any required remedial work and provide written confirmation.

questions.prompt: The IET-recommended interval is fundamentally a starting point because:

options.A: The duty holder owns in-service safety and adjusts the interval based on actual conditions, occupation and previous reports
options.B: The Regulations leave the choice to the inspector alone
options.D: There is no legal requirement to act on the recommendation

questions.explanation: GN3 intervals provide a defensible starting point. The duty holder retains responsibility for in-service safety and is expected to shorten the interval where conditions, alterations, environment or previous findings justify it.

questions.prompt: A rental caravan unit (the caravan itself, not the pitch supply) — recommended IET periodic inspection interval:

options.B: 3 years

questions.explanation: The rental caravan is 1 year — its installation is exposed to road vibration, frequent connection cycles and intensive short-let use. The pitch supply is separately treated and is typically on a longer interval.

questions.prompt: A garden centre with outdoor display lighting and a heated greenhouse. Best fit for the recommended interval:

options.A: Treated as agricultural / horticultural — typically 3 years
options.B: Treated as commercial — typically 5 years

questions.explanation: Horticultural premises sit with agricultural in GN3 — the watering, humidity, dust and rough handling drive a shorter interval than general commercial.

questions.prompt: A privately rented HMO in England. Statutory maximum EICR interval under ESS PRS Regs 2020:

options.B: 3 years
options.C: 5 years, or at change of tenancy if sooner

questions.explanation: ESS PRS: 5 years max, with change of tenancy as a trigger if sooner. HMOs may also fall under separate licensing regimes that demand additional checks; the 5-year EICR ceiling still applies.

questions.prompt: A school building containing classrooms, kitchen, a science lab and a small swimming pool. The pool zone interval:

options.B: 3 years

questions.explanation: Special locations follow their own GN3 intervals regardless of the parent building. The pool keeps the 1-year figure even though the rest of the school is on a 5-year commercial cycle.

questions.prompt: Following a flood, the most appropriate response regarding the EICR cycle is:

options.A: Continue on the original interval — the report has not expired
options.B: Trigger an unscheduled periodic inspection because flood damage may have compromised the installation

questions.explanation: Flood, fire, electric shock and major damage are recognised GN3 triggers for an out-of-cycle inspection — the previous report cannot speak to the post-incident condition of the installation.

questions.prompt: An office occupies a unit on a business park. The previous EICR is 4 years old and Satisfactory. The duty holder is asked whether they can extend the interval to 7 years to save cost. The most defensible response is:

options.A: Yes, provided no alterations have been made
options.B: No — the recommended commercial 5-year figure stands as the starting point and is not extended on grounds of cost alone
options.C: Yes — commercial intervals can be doubled by agreement
options.D: Yes — every premises can be extended to 10 years

questions.explanation: Cost is not a recognised reason to extend a recommended interval. The duty holder's case for extending must be based on conditions, low use or compensating measures — and recorded — not on saving money.

questions.prompt: BS 7671 651.1 objectives include 'protection against damage to property by fire and heat'. In an EICR context this typically means checking:

options.B: Compatibility of protective devices with conductor sizes, signs of overheating, suitable enclosures, and proper segregation
options.D: The age of the consumer unit

questions.explanation: Fire/heat protection on an EICR translates to evidence of correct device coordination, no signs of overheating at terminations, suitable enclosures, mechanical protection and segregation. It is not about looks or age in isolation.

questions.prompt: A privately rented home in England has been let. The previous EICR is 6 years old. Under ESS PRS Regs 2020 the landlord:

options.A: Has breached the 5-year max and must commission a fresh EICR
options.B: Is fine because the report covers 10 years
options.C: Is exempt because the property has been let continuously
options.D: Can defer until the next change of tenancy

questions.explanation: ESS PRS 2020: 5-year max. Letting with an out-of-date EICR breaches the Regulations — the landlord risks enforcement and a financial penalty from the local authority.

questions.prompt: Periodic inspection of an installation owned by a self-employed sole trader operating from a home workshop:

options.A: Falls outside EAWR because it is a domestic property
options.B: Falls within EAWR because work activity is being carried out — the workshop part should be treated like a workplace
options.C: Is governed only by the PRS Regs
options.D: Is voluntary because the trader owns the building

questions.explanation: EAWR follows work activity, not building label. Where a domestic building is also a workplace (workshop, home office with employees, B&B), the workplace part is subject to EAWR maintenance duties as well as any domestic regime.

questions.prompt: Petrol filling station forecourt with HV CHP generation: recommended interval for the LV installation:

options.B: 3 years

questions.explanation: Petrol stations are 1 year — hazardous-area classification, ignition consequences, and constant public traffic justify the shortest practical interval. The HV side is governed separately by the operator's HV maintenance regime.

questions.prompt: An EICR is being scoped for a hotel that was last inspected 4 years ago. There is a swimming pool, a kitchen, and standard guest rooms. The most defensible interval recommendation for the next cycle is:

options.B: 5-year cycle for the hotel as a whole, with the swimming pool zone and kitchen on shorter intervals reflecting their special locations and use
options.C: 10-year cycle to match an owner-occupied dwelling
options.D: 3-month cycle as if it were a construction site

questions.explanation: Mixed-use buildings get a primary commercial interval with shorter sub-intervals for special locations (pools, saunas, kitchens). GN3 intervals are starting points and are tailored area-by-area.

questions.prompt: Recommended GN3 inspection interval for a fish farm:

options.B: 3 years

questions.explanation: Fish farms are 1 year — extensive water-handling, aerators, immersion-rated fittings and continuous environmental stress place them with the highest-risk LV environments alongside marinas, pools and petrol stations.

questions.prompt: An EICR is Unsatisfactory because of a single C2 observation. The duty holder under EAWR has to:

options.A: Take reasonable action to remove the danger as soon as practicable, in line with the inspector's recommendation
options.B: Wait for the next inspection cycle
options.C: Disregard the C2 because it is not a C1

questions.explanation: C2 = potentially dangerous and must be acted on. EAWR's duty to maintain so as to prevent danger applies — the action must be reasonable, proportionate and timely, and the report Unsatisfactory until resolved.

questions.prompt: Building Regulations Part P applies to:

options.B: Notifiable electrical work in dwellings in England

questions.explanation: Part P is a Building Regulations duty for notifiable electrical work in dwellings (England). It is not a periodic-inspection regime — its role is to control new and altered work in domestic premises.

questions.prompt: A shop in a commercial parade has reduced its trading days to weekends only. The EICR interval can:

options.B: Be reviewed by the duty holder against actual reduced use, but a strong case must be evidenced and recorded if extending past 5 years
options.C: Be ignored because the unit is closed midweek

questions.explanation: Reduced occupancy is a recognised factor in interval setting. The duty holder may justify a slightly longer interval but must record the rationale; the GN3 5-year figure is the defensible starting point.

questions.prompt: Privately rented dwellings: enforcement under ESS PRS Regs 2020 sits with:

options.B: The local authority for the area where the property is located

questions.explanation: ESS PRS 2020 is enforced by the local authority. They can demand the EICR within 7 days, request remedial confirmation, take remedial action themselves and recover costs, and impose a financial penalty up to £30,000.

questions.prompt: A 25-year-old public-house lounge bar with no recent EICR on file. The most defensible response is to:

options.A: Treat it as commercial and apply a 5-year starting interval, but with a fresh EICR now and risk-based shortening if condition warrants
options.B: Wait for a complaint
options.D: Apply 25 years to match the building age

questions.explanation: Public houses are commercial; 5 years is the GN3 starting point. With no recent EICR, the priority is to commission one now and let the findings drive the next interval.

questions.prompt: An EAWR-driven duty holder argues that they only need an EICR every 25 years because the building has been continuously occupied. This position is:

options.A: Correct — long occupancy justifies long intervals
options.B: Incorrect — EAWR's duty to maintain is continuous and an EICR every 25 years is well outside any GN3 figure for any building type
options.C: Correct, provided the original EIC is on file
options.D: Correct as long as PAT testing is up to date

questions.explanation: Continuous occupation does not extend GN3 intervals to 25 years. EAWR demands maintenance to prevent danger, supported by periodic inspection at recognised intervals. PAT testing covers portable appliances, not the fixed installation.

questions.prompt: A fire was caused by a deteriorated joint in the consumer unit. The premises are commercial. The most appropriate next step regarding periodic inspection is:

options.B: Trigger an unscheduled EICR to assess wider damage and verify the rest of the installation
options.C: Cancel the EICR cycle because the consumer unit will be replaced
options.D: Refer the matter to the DNO

questions.explanation: Fire is a recognised trigger for an unscheduled periodic inspection. Even after the failed component is replaced, the wider installation needs verifying — the heat may have compromised neighbouring conductors and accessories.

questions.prompt: The legal driver behind periodic inspection in privately rented dwellings in England (since 2020) is most precisely:

options.B: The Electrical Safety Standards in the Private Rented Sector (England) Regulations 2020, complemented by the duty in HSWA where the landlord is a business

questions.explanation: ESS PRS 2020 made periodic inspection a statutory duty on landlords in England (5-yearly max, 28-day remedial duty, copy to tenant within 28 days). HSWA still applies to landlords operating as a business; EAWR primarily applies to workplaces.

questions.prompt: A community centre hosting children's parties, fitness classes and an over-60s club. Most defensible starting interval:

options.B: 3 years (treated as a place of public assembly, with judgement adjustment)

questions.explanation: Places of public assembly typically sit at 1-3 years in GN3. The duty holder uses judgement on actual occupation; light-use community halls are usually defensible at the longer end of the band, never at domestic figures.

questions.prompt: A rental caravan-park pitch socket installation: recommended IET maximum interval:

options.B: 3 years

questions.explanation: Pitch sockets are typically 3 years. The rental caravan unit itself is 1 year. The two are commonly conflated — keep them separate when scoping the EICR.

questions.prompt: A landlord has just received an EICR with a single C3 observation. Under ESS PRS Regs 2020 the report is:

options.A: Unsatisfactory and remedial work is statutory
options.B: Satisfactory — C3 alone does not make a report Unsatisfactory or trigger the 28-day remedial duty
options.C: Unsatisfactory because all coded observations are statutory

questions.explanation: C3 (improvement recommended) does not in itself make the report Unsatisfactory. The 28-day remedial duty under ESS PRS is triggered by C1, C2 or FI — not C3.

questions.prompt: A 10-year-old privately rented house has its periodic EICR carried out. The previous landlord did not commission an EICR. Action required by ESS PRS 2020 is:

options.A: Wait until the property is empty
options.B: Commission the EICR immediately and supply the report to the tenant within 28 days; act on any C1/C2/FI within the further 28-day window
options.D: Wait until the home is sold

questions.explanation: ESS PRS Regs are statutory in England — every privately rented dwelling must have a current EICR. New landlords inheriting a property without one must commission an inspection without delay and meet the supply and remedial timescales.

questions.prompt: A small car repair workshop. The duty holder asks whether the agricultural 3-year interval applies because the building was once a barn. The defensible answer is:

options.B: No — current use governs the interval; an industrial unit is typically 3 years and a small commercial garage is around 3-5 years depending on use
options.C: Yes — buildings keep their original interval

questions.explanation: Current use sets the interval. Industrial premises are 3 years and small commercial garages typically run 3-5 years depending on the work. The previous use of the building does not transfer.

questions.prompt: An EICR was commissioned for an industrial unit on a 3-year cycle. The previous report had two C2 observations. For the next interval the duty holder should:

options.A: Extend the interval to 5 years for compensation
options.B: Maintain or shorten the 3-year cycle until repeat findings are stable; record the justification on the new EICR
options.D: Keep the same interval but only inspect half the circuits

questions.explanation: Previous findings drive the next interval. Recurring C2s suggest under-investment or harsh service; the duty holder maintains or shortens the cycle and records the rationale for the next EICR.

questions.prompt: Recommended IET maximum interval for a public swimming pool plant room (the room with pumps, dosing and switchgear):

options.B: 3 years

questions.explanation: Swimming pool installations are 1 year, including the plant area. Chemical atmospheres (chlorine, bromine), humidity and continuous public footfall add up to one of the highest-risk LV environments.

questions.prompt: Periodic inspection in the workplace is principally driven by:

options.B: EAWR 1989 (Reg 4(2)) and HSWA 1974, with BS 7671 / GN3 as the recognised technical means of compliance
options.D: The Construction (Design and Management) Regulations only

questions.explanation: EAWR + HSWA provide the legal driver; BS 7671 and GN3 provide the recognised technical means. Part P is dwellings only, RIDDOR is incident reporting, CDM is construction. None of those replace EAWR for periodic verification in a workplace.

questions.prompt: A school is planning its EICR. The starting GN3 interval to apply is typically:

options.B: 3 years

questions.explanation: Schools are usually treated as commercial (5 years) for the main building, with shorter sub-intervals for special locations (kitchens, swimming pools, science labs) where the use justifies them.

questions.prompt: A duty holder argues that the EICR is the inspector's responsibility, not theirs. The defensible position is:

options.A: Correct — once commissioned the inspector owns the duty
options.B: Incorrect — the duty holder retains the legal duty under EAWR / ESS PRS; the EICR is evidence of due diligence, not a transfer of responsibility
options.C: Correct because the inspector signs the report
options.D: Correct because the inspector is qualified

questions.explanation: EAWR and ESS PRS place the duty on the duty holder (employer / landlord). The EICR is evidence the duty has been discharged. Commissioning the inspection does not move the legal responsibility off the duty holder.

questions.prompt: An owner-occupier has had an EICR voluntarily, returning Satisfactory with one C3. The recommended next inspection date is:

options.B: 3 years
options.C: 5-10 years (typically 10 years for owner-occupied, with the inspector's specific recommendation on the report)

questions.explanation: Owner-occupied is up to 10 years in GN3, but the inspector states the recommended date on the report. C3 alone does not shorten the interval, but the inspector may still recommend earlier where condition warrants.

questions.prompt: An EICR records the words 'extent and limitations agreed in writing with the duty holder before the inspection commenced'. The point of doing this is:

options.B: To make clear which parts of the installation are inside the scope of the report and which are not — protecting both parties' liability
options.C: To allow the inspector to skip live testing

questions.explanation: Agreeing extent and limitations defines the scope of the report. Anything outside the agreed scope is excluded from the conclusions and the duty holder accepts that. It is the foundation of defensible PIT documentation.

questions.prompt: A hotel with a swimming pool fails its 5-year EICR (Unsatisfactory). The hotel manager asks whether they can keep operating until remedial work is completed. The most defensible response is:

options.B: Address C1 immediately (and write to the duty holder); plan C2 within a reasonable timescale and complete FI without delay; keep the affected high-risk areas off until danger has been removed
options.C: Close the entire hotel until the next EICR
options.D: Continue trading and re-test in 12 months

questions.explanation: Unsatisfactory does not require closing the building, but it requires acting on the codes proportionately. C1 demands immediate action. C2 must be planned and completed promptly. Specific dangerous circuits (e.g. the pool) may need isolating until the work is done.

questions.prompt: Recommended periodic inspection interval for a leisure centre with pool, gym, sauna and changing rooms:

options.A: Single 1-year cycle for the whole building
options.B: 1 year for the pool/sauna/special locations and 3-5 years for the main building (mixed-use approach)

questions.explanation: Mixed-use leisure centres are typically scoped on a tiered basis — special locations on 1-year, main building on 3-5 years. The single global figure rarely fits a mixed building.

questions.prompt: GN3 lists triggers for an out-of-cycle (unscheduled) periodic inspection. Which of these is NOT a recognised trigger?

options.B: Flood
options.C: Decision by the duty holder to repaint the walls
options.D: Significant damage or an electric shock incident

questions.explanation: Triggers are condition or risk-driven (fire, flood, shock, major damage, change of use). Decorative changes do not normally trigger an unscheduled periodic inspection.

questions.prompt: A duty holder asks whether they can use the previous EICR to carry forward the same Unsatisfactory observations to the new report. The defensible position is:

options.A: Yes — paste the previous defects forward
options.B: No — the new EICR is a fresh assessment based on current observations and tests; previous reports are background only
options.C: Yes, only the C3s carry forward
options.D: Yes, only the FI items carry forward

questions.explanation: Each EICR is a snapshot in time based on the current inspection. Previous reports inform context (history, recurring issues) but they do not pre-populate the new findings.

questions.prompt: A housing association lets a privately rented dwelling. The dwelling has a small commercial office on the ground floor (mixed use). The defensible interval position is:

options.A: Treat the whole property as 5 years (PRS Regs minimum)
options.B: Treat the whole property as 10 years (domestic)
options.C: Apply 5 years to the residential element under ESS PRS, and assess the commercial element under EAWR/GN3 commercial 5-year, with overall scoping of the EICR

questions.explanation: Mixed-use properties get parallel treatment — ESS PRS for the residential part, EAWR/GN3 for the commercial part. Both happen to land on 5 years here, but the legal driver and the documentation are tracked separately.

questions.prompt: A privately rented dwelling EICR returns Unsatisfactory with one C1 and three C2s. ESS PRS Regs require remedial completion within:

options.A: 28 days, or sooner where the inspector specifies
options.B: 3 months

questions.explanation: ESS PRS 2020: 28-day remedial duty, or sooner where specified. The inspector commonly specifies 'immediate' for a C1 and the landlord must obtain written confirmation of completion.

questions.prompt: BS 7671 Reg 651.1 defines what periodic inspection is for. Critically, it says the inspection is to verify safety so far as:

options.B: The original installer can attend

questions.explanation: 'So far as reasonably practicable' is the qualifier — it links Reg 651.1 to HSWA/EAWR thinking. The inspection cannot guarantee zero defects but must take reasonable steps to verify the four safety objectives.

questions.prompt: A duty holder claims that periodic inspection only matters where there has been a problem. The defensible position is:

options.A: Correct — no problem means no inspection
options.B: Incorrect — periodic inspection is a proactive condition assessment carried out at recognised intervals so problems are detected before they cause harm
options.C: Correct — only the DNO requires periodic inspection
options.D: Correct — only insurers require periodic inspection

questions.explanation: PIT is proactive. Without it, deterioration only surfaces when something fails — typically a fire, a shock or an enforcement action. The recognised intervals exist precisely because deterioration is gradual and otherwise invisible.

questions.prompt: A privately rented dwelling EICR is being commissioned. The landlord tells the inspector to skip the kitchen because the tenant is cooking. The defensible response is:

options.B: Record the kitchen as a limitation, explain that anything not inspected is outside the report, and ask the landlord to arrange access for a follow-up if needed

questions.explanation: Operational restrictions become limitations in EICR Section D. The duty holder accepts that the un-inspected area is outside the conclusions. The inspector communicates the implication and may recommend a follow-up.

questions.prompt: GN3 recommended interval for general industrial premises:

options.B: 3 years

questions.explanation: Industrial premises are typically 3 years. Heavier service conditions, higher mechanical and thermal stress, and larger installations all justify a shorter interval than general commercial.

questions.prompt: An EICR is being scoped for a small bakery (commercial). Its cellar contains a 3-phase distribution board feeding ovens that cannot be switched off without spoiling stock. The most defensible response is:

options.B: Agree extended dead-test out of hours; if not feasible, agree limitations or use appropriate live tests with the duty holder's written agreement and document accordingly
options.C: Test the ovens with their doors open

questions.explanation: Continuous-process loads need a planned approach — out-of-hours dead testing, partial sampling, agreed live tests where dead testing isn't reasonably practicable. The route chosen is recorded in extent and limitations.

questions.prompt: A new owner of an owner-occupied dwelling commissions an EICR voluntarily. They ask the inspector to write 'change of occupancy inspection'. This is:

options.A: Inappropriate — it implies a regime that doesn't exist for owner-occupiers
options.B: Defensible — change of occupancy is a recognised GN3 trigger and recording it on the EICR is good practice

questions.explanation: GN3 names change of occupancy as a recommended trigger for an EICR even on owner-occupied homes. The trigger is voluntary in legal terms, but documenting the rationale strengthens the report.

questions.prompt: Recommended IET maximum interval for a place of public entertainment such as a music venue:

options.B: 3 years

questions.explanation: Places of public entertainment, theatres and similar are commonly 1 year. Public access, heavy temporary lighting and sound, and event-driven mechanical abuse drive the short interval.

questions.prompt: A privately rented HMO has an EICR commissioned. The local authority requests a copy. The landlord must supply it within:

options.B: 14 days

questions.explanation: ESS PRS 2020: local authority can request the EICR and the landlord must supply it within 7 days. Existing tenants get 28 days; new tenants get the report before they move in.

questions.prompt: Construction site temporary supply: GN3 recommended interval is:

options.B: 1 year

questions.explanation: Construction site supplies are typically 3 months. Temporary cabling, exposed sockets, frequent reconfiguration and weather all add up to a high failure rate without short cycles.

questions.prompt: A commercial customer asks whether an EICR is mandatory for them. The defensible response is:

options.B: An EICR is not mandated by name, but EAWR Reg 4(2) and HSWA require maintenance to prevent danger, and an EICR at GN3 intervals is the recognised means of demonstrating compliance
options.C: No — only domestic premises need EICRs
options.D: Only if the local authority asks

questions.explanation: BS 7671 doesn't make the EICR statutory by itself. EAWR places the duty; the EICR is the recognised technical means. Workplaces that ignore periodic inspection are exposed under EAWR and HSWA.

questions.prompt: A previously satisfactory EICR has expired by 6 months on a privately rented home in England. ESS PRS Regs are:

options.B: Strict — the 5-year max is a statutory ceiling and a fresh EICR should be commissioned without further delay

questions.explanation: ESS PRS 2020: 5-year max is statutory. The duty holder is in breach as soon as the date is exceeded; a fresh EICR must be commissioned, and enforcement is at local-authority discretion.

questions.prompt: An office tenant complains they cannot have their power interrupted at all. The defensible PIT approach is:

options.B: Plan dead testing out of hours, sample where appropriate, agree limitations for what cannot be reached, and document — live testing only where dead testing isn't reasonably practicable

questions.explanation: Out-of-hours work, agreed sampling, and clear limitations are the standard tools for power-sensitive offices. Live testing remains an exception, justified case-by-case and recorded.

questions.prompt: Cinema (auditorium and lobby): recommended IET interval:

options.B: 3 years

questions.explanation: Cinemas typically 3 years. Some places of public assembly (theatres, music venues) are pushed to 1 year due to public access and event-driven service conditions, but cinemas are usually on 3 years.

questions.prompt: An owner-occupied dwelling alters use partially to a B&B with three letting rooms. The property is now:

options.B: A workplace under EAWR for the B&B portion, in addition to its domestic regime — and the EICR cycle should reflect that
options.D: Required only to comply with Part P

questions.explanation: EAWR follows work activity. A home that takes paying guests is partly a workplace and the EICR scoping should reflect both regimes. Domestic and commercial intervals may both apply to different parts.

questions.prompt: A school's EICR has just expired. The headteacher asks whether term-time use justifies a short delay. The defensible response is:

options.B: No — the duty under EAWR continues; commission the inspection without further delay and plan around school holidays where practicable
options.C: Yes — but only to the next school holiday
options.D: Yes — by writing to the DfE

questions.explanation: EAWR is continuous. Term-time pressure justifies planning, not deferring. Schools commonly schedule EICRs in school holidays — the duty itself does not pause.

questions.prompt: A customer asks whether the EICR pass mark is the same as initial verification. The defensible response is:

options.B: No — initial verification produces an EIC issued for new work; an EICR is a Satisfactory/Unsatisfactory condition report on existing work, with C-codes / FI / Schedule of Test Results
options.D: Yes — both are valid for 10 years

questions.explanation: Initial verification certifies new/altered work via the EIC; periodic verification reports condition via the EICR with C-codes and FI. The two regimes have different documents, different drivers, and different acceptance criteria.

questions.prompt: An EAWR duty holder argues that periodic inspection at GN3 intervals is 'just guidance' and so optional. The defensible position is:

options.B: GN3 is non-statutory in itself, but it is the recognised means of demonstrating compliance with EAWR Reg 4(2) — ignoring it leaves the duty holder exposed without a defensible alternative
options.C: Correct — periodic inspection only matters in dwellings

questions.explanation: GN3 is non-statutory but it is the recognised technical reference. Duty holders departing from it must have an equally defensible alternative — there is none in routine practice.

questions.prompt: A privately rented dwelling has a Satisfactory EICR with no codes. The next mandatory action is:

options.B: Supply a copy to the existing tenant within 28 days; supply to a new tenant before move-in; supply to the local authority within 7 days on request
options.D: File the report and do nothing

questions.explanation: ESS PRS supply duties apply even when the report is Satisfactory. Skipping the supply duty is itself a breach, regardless of the inspection result.

questions.prompt: A new tenant moves into a privately rented dwelling. Under ESS PRS Regs the landlord must:

options.A: Supply the EICR before the tenant moves in
options.B: Supply it any time during the first month

questions.explanation: ESS PRS 2020: new tenants get the EICR before move-in. Existing tenants get it within 28 days. Local authority gets it within 7 days on request. The full report goes — not just a summary.

questions.prompt: A duty holder argues that change of occupancy on an owner-occupied home is statutory. The defensible position is:

options.B: Incorrect — change of occupancy is a GN3-recommended trigger for owner-occupied; it is statutory under ESS PRS only for privately rented dwellings (England)

questions.explanation: Owner-occupied is voluntary; the trigger is recommended in GN3. Privately rented (England) is statutory under ESS PRS 2020 — that is where the legal weight sits.

questions.prompt: A customer asks whether the inspector's professional indemnity covers any later claim. The defensible position is:

options.B: PI provides cover within agreed scope; clear extent and limitations on the EICR define what is and isn't included — anything outside the agreed scope is not warranted by the inspector
options.D: Only if the property is owner-occupied

questions.explanation: Liability follows the agreed scope. A clear extent-and-limitations entry on the EICR is the inspector's primary protection against claims for parts of the installation that were not within the inspection.

questions.prompt: An EAWR-driven duty holder wants to know how short an interval can be set. The defensible response is:

options.A: Intervals must always match the GN3 figure
options.B: GN3 figures are recommended maxima — shorter intervals are perfectly defensible (and sometimes obligatory) where conditions, use or previous findings warrant
options.C: Intervals cannot be shorter than 1 year
options.D: Intervals cannot be shorter than the previous EICR's interval

questions.explanation: GN3 intervals are starting maxima. Shorter cycles are entirely defensible — and required where the condition or use of the installation makes the standard figure too long.

questions.prompt: The agreed EICR extent covers DB2 and DB3 only, not DB1. While inspecting DB2, you see a damaged submain cable leaving DB1 and feeding DB2. What is the best action?

options.A: Ignore it because DB1 was excluded
options.B: Record it only in your private notes, not on the EICR
options.C: Record it as N/A because it originates outside the agreed extent
options.D: Record the unsafe condition because it affects the inspected installation, and notify the client if urgent action is needed

questions.explanation: A damaged submain supplying DB2 is directly relevant to DB2's safety. If live parts are accessible, it may be C1. If insulation, mechanical protection, earthing or fire safety is compromised, it is commonly C2. Excluding DB1 does not permit you to ignore visible danger affecting the included installation.

questions.prompt: A 20% sample of accessories is agreed for a 24-circuit office. On the first sampled socket circuit you find reversed polarity, loose CPCs and signs of overheating. What should happen to the sample?

options.A: Keep the 20% sample unchanged because it was agreed before work started
options.B: Increase the sample, potentially to 100% of that circuit and a greater sample of similar circuits
options.C: Stop recording defects after the first one because the report is already unsatisfactory
options.D: Downgrade the defects to C3 because they were found during sampling

questions.explanation: Sampling is based on confidence. Early serious defects destroy confidence in the original sample. Reversed polarity and loose CPCs are normally C2, and overheating is usually C2 unless it presents immediate danger. The limitation should be revised or the client's refusal to expand the sample should be recorded.

questions.prompt: Before testing, you remove a consumer unit cover and find an exposed live busbar finger due to a missing protective shroud. The installation is occupied. What is the most appropriate immediate response?

options.A: Stop, prevent access, make safe where possible, notify the occupier/client immediately, and record the danger
options.B: Continue testing because the defect can be written up later
options.C: Record C3 because the cover was removed by a skilled person
options.D: Record N/V because inspection could not continue

questions.explanation: Immediate danger must be controlled before you continue or leave site. If live parts are accessible in normal use, the classification is C1. If exposure exists only when a tool-required cover is removed, the exact code depends on access and circumstances, but the condition must still be made safe for inspection and maintenance.

questions.prompt: Which mapping best distinguishes N/V, LIM, FI and N/A?

options.A: Locked roof void = FI; nonexistent swimming pool = C3; unidentified circuit = N/A; sensitive equipment left connected = C1
options.B: Locked roof void = LIM/N/V; nonexistent swimming pool = N/A; unidentified circuit = FI or N/V for uncompleted tests; sensitive equipment preventing L-N insulation testing = LIM/N/V with the reason stated
options.C: All untested items should be C2
options.D: N/V and FI mean exactly the same thing

questions.explanation: A limitation is an agreed or operational restriction. N/V means not verified. FI means the inspector cannot determine safety without further investigation. N/A means the item does not apply. A locked void is a limitation; a nonexistent swimming pool is N/A; an unidentified circuit may need FI; and connected sensitive equipment is a limitation on that test.

questions.prompt: An EICR for a 12-floor office tower is being scoped. The duty holder asks for sampling to keep the cost reasonable. The defensible position is:

options.A: Sampling is a cost decision and the inspector defers to the client
options.B: Sampling is a risk decision: agree a representative sample (typically 10-20% of repeating accessories), retain 100% on origins/switchgear, and document the basis in writing

questions.explanation: Sampling is a risk decision. Origin and main switchgear stay 100%. Repeating accessories sample at typical 10-20% rates, increased on findings. The basis is documented in writing as part of extent and limitations.

questions.prompt: The inspector samples sockets on a busy retail floor and finds the same loose terminal on two of the ten sampled. The defensible response is:

options.B: Increase the sample, expand testing toward 100% if the pattern continues, and code each defect appropriately (typically C2 for loose terminations creating a potential connection failure)
options.C: Ignore the loose terminations because they were not in the agreed sample
options.D: Issue Unsatisfactory and refer to the DNO

questions.explanation: Repeating defects justify expanding the sample. Loose terminations in busy areas typically code C2 (potentially dangerous — risk of arcing and overheating) and the inspector documents the wider check.

questions.prompt: Live testing is justified only when:

options.A: The duty holder offers to pay extra
options.B: Dead testing is not reasonably practicable, the duty holder accepts the residual risk, GS38-compliant test leads and PPE are used, and the rationale is recorded on the EICR
options.C: The inspector cannot find an isolation point
options.D: The installation is more than 5 years old

questions.explanation: Dead test by default. Live testing happens only where dead testing isn't reasonably practicable. The case must be specific, the duty holder must accept the residual risk, and the rationale and method are recorded.

questions.prompt: Sampling that turns up a defect on a single circuit suggests:

options.B: An expansion of the sample within the same group; the size of the expansion depends on the consequence and the rate of similar findings

questions.explanation: Sampling escalation is risk-based. A single defect doesn't automatically force 100%, but the sample expands and continues until the inspector is reasonably confident the population is understood.

questions.prompt: EICR Section D ('extent and limitations') is the place to record:

options.B: Areas not inspected, agreed sampling, items the duty holder asked the inspector to leave for cost or operational reasons, and the rationale for each

questions.explanation: Section D is the documentation of scope. Areas excluded, sampling levels, operational restrictions and the rationale all go here. It is the inspector's primary protection on liability.

questions.prompt: Limitations cannot legitimately be used to:

options.B: Cover a circuit that could not be isolated during the visit
options.C: Hide an observed danger because the duty holder asks for it to be omitted
options.D: Note that part of the building was tenanted and locked

questions.explanation: Limitations record genuine restrictions. Once an inspector has observed a danger, it must be coded — limitations cannot be used as a hiding place for an observed defect, even at the duty holder's request.

questions.prompt: Out-of-hours dead testing on a 24/7 facility is preferable because:

options.B: Dead testing is the safer default and meeting it requires planning around occupancy; live testing introduces additional shock and arc-flash risk
options.C: It allows the inspector to skip live tests

questions.explanation: Dead testing is the GN3 default. Out-of-hours work is the planning route to honour that on continuous-process sites. Live testing remains an exception, justified case-by-case.

questions.prompt: A privately rented dwelling EICR has a clear, signed extent-and-limitations entry. The benefit of this is:

options.B: Defines the scope of the report so anything outside it is excluded from the conclusions; both parties understand who is responsible for what

questions.explanation: A signed Section D protects both sides. The duty holder accepts what was excluded; the inspector limits liability to the agreed scope. It is the documentary backbone of a defensible EICR.

questions.prompt: An inspector cannot dead-test a continuous-process line. Acceptable approaches include:

options.B: Plan a maintenance shutdown for dead test, or agree limited live tests with the duty holder, or treat untestable items as limitations and recommend a follow-up window

questions.explanation: The standard playbook: plan a shutdown, agree a defined live-test scope where shutdown is impossible, or agree limitations. The choice is documented and the duty holder accepts the residual risk.

questions.prompt: A 100-circuit installation is sampled at 10%. Two sampled circuits return low IR. The next defensible step is:

options.B: Investigate the two faulted circuits, expand the sample, and code accordingly; if the cause cannot be diagnosed during the visit, raise FI

questions.explanation: Repeated low IR triggers expansion. The inspector investigates, escalates the sample, and uses FI if the cause cannot be located during the visit. The report becomes Unsatisfactory until resolved.

questions.prompt: An EICR records 'sampling: 100% of consumer units, 20% of socket outlets, 100% of fire alarm circuits, lighting in occupied areas only'. This kind of mixed sampling is:

options.B: Defensible — different items get different sample sizes based on their risk profile, with origin/critical systems at 100%
options.D: Wrong — sampling never includes consumer units

questions.explanation: Sampling is per-group, not uniform. Critical/safety systems and origins go to 100%. Repeating sockets and lights sample at lower rates. The mixed approach reflects the real risk profile.

questions.prompt: Failure to obtain a written agreement on extent and limitations exposes the inspector because:

options.A: The DNO can demand the report
options.B: The report appears to cover the whole installation, so anything subsequently found defective could be argued to be within the inspector's scope and judgement
options.C: The local authority is automatically notified

questions.explanation: Without written extent and limitations, the report appears comprehensive. If something later goes wrong on an un-tested circuit, the inspector has no documentary basis for excluding it from the EICR's conclusions.

questions.prompt: An EICR limitation that says 'the basement boiler room could not be inspected because the key holder was unavailable' is:

options.A: Acceptable — record it in Section D and recommend follow-up access
options.B: Unacceptable — the inspector should break in
options.C: Acceptable only if the boiler is small
options.D: Acceptable only if the duty holder waives all liability

questions.explanation: Genuine access restrictions are legitimate limitations. The inspector records the reason, recommends a follow-up to complete the un-inspected scope, and the duty holder accepts that it is outside the report's conclusions.

questions.prompt: An EICR sample turns up a recurring 6242Y cable type used in a damp area. The defensible response is:

options.B: Investigate further, expand the sample to other parts of the same area, code per the actual condition (C2 if damage / risk; C3 if compliant but improvement-recommended), and document the area-wide finding

questions.explanation: Pattern findings demand expansion. The inspector investigates, expands the sample, and codes against actual condition. Documenting the whole area helps the duty holder plan remedial work.

questions.prompt: An office EICR has 'sampling: 20% of similar circuits' agreed. During testing, no defects are found. The defensible record is:

options.A: Issue Satisfactory; document the sample size, the result and the un-sampled population in Section D
options.B: Re-test 100% just in case
options.D: Issue Unsatisfactory because not everything was tested

questions.explanation: When the agreed sample passes, the report is Satisfactory but the documentation in Section D is critical — the un-sampled circuits are explicitly outside the conclusions and the duty holder accepts that.

questions.prompt: An office tenant insists computers must not be turned off. The defensible response is:

options.B: Agree out-of-hours dead testing where possible, agree limitations on what cannot be reached, and document any specific live tests in Section D and the test results schedule

questions.explanation: Continuous-IT environments are common. Plan dead testing out-of-hours, agree limitations for the rest, and document any live tests. The duty holder accepts the residual position in writing.

questions.prompt: An EICR sample reveals one C1 defect (immediate danger). The inspector should:

options.B: Take immediate action to make safe (or warn / isolate), notify the duty holder in writing immediately, then continue with an expanded sample focused on related items
options.C: Wait until the report is written

questions.explanation: C1 demands immediate action and same-day written notification (BPG4). The inspector then continues with an expanded sample, aware that the original defect rate may have been understated.

questions.prompt: A duty holder asks for the EICR to be split into 'phases' so only some circuits are tested per visit. The defensible response is:

options.B: Phased inspections are a recognised approach for very large installations; agree the phasing in writing as the extent for each phase, with each phase producing its own EICR or a clearly scoped report
options.C: Test everything in one visit regardless
options.D: Issue a single EICR but date it differently

questions.explanation: Phased EICRs are common on large estates. Each phase has its own clearly scoped extent and limitations. The duty holder must understand that areas in future phases are not yet covered.

questions.prompt: A live-tested circuit returns a Zs reading at the upper end of the table value. The defensible response is:

options.B: Apply the GN3 80% measured-value rule of thumb and investigate any reading near or above the limit; check ambient temperature correction and re-test cold if practical

questions.explanation: GN3's 80% rule of thumb says measured Zs near or above 80% of the table value warrants investigation, because conductors heat up in service. Live tests already include ambient temperature, so a borderline reading typically demands further check.

questions.prompt: An agreed limitation must:

options.A: Be documented in Section D with the reason, agreed with the duty holder, and not conceal an observed danger
options.B: Be added at the inspector's sole discretion
options.D: Cover any circuit the inspector would rather not test

questions.explanation: Limitations are documented (Section D), agreed (duty holder), explained (reason). They cannot be used to hide observed danger; once a defect is seen, it is coded — never hidden behind a limitation.

questions.prompt: An inspector samples 10% of socket outlets and finds 3 of 10 with reversed polarity. The defensible response is:

options.B: Increase the sample size sharply, code each finding (typically C2 for reversed polarity), and report the wider pattern; the inspector may move to 100% on the affected circuit group
options.C: Issue Satisfactory because it is only polarity

questions.explanation: 30% defect rate triggers a sharp expansion. Reversed polarity is typically C2 (potentially dangerous — accessories rely on neutral being switched/protected correctly). The pattern justifies extending to 100% on the affected group.

questions.prompt: Live testing PPE and instrument requirements are governed by:

options.B: GS38 (test leads/probes), HSE guidance on live working PPE, the inspector's risk assessment, and the duty holder's site safety rules

questions.explanation: GS38 covers test leads/probes; HSE / EAWR cover live working PPE; site rules add controls. Appendix 4 is design (volt drop), Part P is dwellings, ESS PRS is privately rented dwellings — none of those cover live testing safety.

questions.prompt: An EICR Section D entry that says 'all circuits tested at 100%' could be unrealistic on a large installation because:

options.B: Genuinely testing every circuit on a very large installation is impracticable; over-stating the scope inflates the inspector's exposure beyond what was actually covered

questions.explanation: Honest scoping is the protection. Over-stating that everything was tested when it wasn't extends liability to circuits that were never visited. Sampling — agreed and documented — is more defensible than a blanket '100%' claim that doesn't match reality.

questions.prompt: An inspector cannot inspect a busy hospital ward. The defensible response is:

options.B: Treat the ward as a limitation, record the reason ('clinical activity, no isolation possible during the visit'), and recommend a follow-up visit out of hours
options.C: Issue Unsatisfactory just for the ward

questions.explanation: Operational limitations on critical environments are textbook Section D entries. The inspector documents the reason, recommends a follow-up, and the duty holder is clear that the ward is not within the report's conclusions.

questions.prompt: The inspector decides to sample 5% of identical socket circuits in a large warehouse. The duty holder is comfortable with this. The defensible record is:

options.A: Record the agreed sample size, the rationale, and the un-sampled circuits in Section D, with the duty holder's signed acceptance
options.B: Test it silently and move on
options.D: Sample 5% but tell the duty holder verbally only

questions.explanation: Section D records the sample, rationale and un-sampled population. Signed acceptance from the duty holder is the documentary safety net. Verbal-only agreements offer none of the legal protection.

questions.prompt: On a sampled circuit, the inspector finds an unsleeved CPC at the consumer unit. The defensible response is:

options.B: Code the finding (typically C3 for missing sleeving), check the rest of the consumer unit, and investigate whether the same workmanship applies elsewhere; expand sampling if pattern is suspected

questions.explanation: Missing sleeving alone is typically C3 (improvement). The presence of one defect prompts a check elsewhere — workmanship issues are usually consistent, and the EICR should reflect the wider pattern.

questions.prompt: An EICR limitation reads 'sockets behind built-in furniture not inspected'. This is:

options.A: Defensible, provided the limitation is recorded with the reason and the duty holder is aware that those sockets are outside the report
options.B: Indefensible — every socket must be inspected
options.D: Defensible only if the furniture is metal

questions.explanation: Genuine access restrictions are valid limitations. Recording them in Section D, with the reason, makes the report's scope clear. Built-in furniture is a common real-world limitation.

questions.prompt: A duty holder offers the inspector a fee uplift to pass an installation that would otherwise be Unsatisfactory. The defensible response is:

options.B: Refuse — the EICR records actual condition; no fee can change a coded observation; raising it as a concern is appropriate
options.C: Accept and add a discreet C3

questions.explanation: Coding integrity is non-negotiable. The inspector records what is observed regardless of payment offers — and treats the offer itself as a serious professional issue.

questions.prompt: Sampling escalation is fundamentally about:

options.B: Confidence — the sample size grows until the inspector can reasonably conclude that the un-sampled population is understood

questions.explanation: The aim of sampling is to give the duty holder a defensible view of the wider population. When confidence is low (high failure rate, complex installation), the sample grows; when confidence is high, the sample stays small.

questions.prompt: An EICR records 'lighting circuits not isolated; live tests applied' on a continuously-occupied call centre. This entry is:

options.A: Defensible, provided the reason for not isolating is given, the live-test method is named, and the duty holder accepts the residual risk in writing
options.B: Indefensible regardless of context

questions.explanation: Live testing where dead testing isn't reasonably practicable is allowed when reason, method and acceptance are documented. The default principle remains dead testing — live testing is the documented exception.

questions.prompt: An EICR sample tested at 20% returns no defects and the un-sampled population is similar in age and type. The defensible recommendation for the next inspection cycle is:

options.A: Continue with 20% sampling, clearly recorded, with no immediate change in interval
options.B: Move to 100% next time

questions.explanation: When the sample is satisfactory, the next cycle can continue with the same sampling rate, clearly recorded. The interval is unchanged unless conditions or use have shifted; the sampling rate is similarly stable until findings drive a change.

questions.prompt: An inspector cannot test a critical control circuit in continuous use. The defensible record is:

options.A: Limitation in Section D, with reason 'continuous-process control circuit; no isolation window agreed during this visit', plus FI if there is a specific concern that cannot be diagnosed without isolation
options.B: Test it live without comment
options.D: Issue Unsatisfactory based on no test data

questions.explanation: Limitation + FI when warranted is the textbook treatment. The duty holder is left with a clear picture: the circuit was not tested, why, and what specific concern (if any) needs follow-up.

questions.prompt: An EICR sample is 'all of one type of repeating accessory'. This is:

options.A: Inappropriate sampling — origin and main switchgear should also be 100%, not just one accessory type
options.B: Acceptable — sampling can be by type

questions.explanation: Sampling by accessory type or circuit family is normal. The phrase 'repeating accessory' implies a homogeneous population — sampling within that group is defensible. Origin and main switchgear are separately covered at 100%.

questions.prompt: An EICR has no Section D entry. The implication is:

options.A: The report is incomplete — Section D is required to record extent and limitations and its absence undermines the report's defensibility
options.B: The report is fine — Section D is optional
options.C: The report is fine if it's a domestic property
options.D: The report is fine if no codes are raised

questions.explanation: Section D records extent and limitations and is a required part of the EICR set. Without it, scope is undefined and the inspector's exposure is at maximum; the report cannot be considered complete.

questions.prompt: An EICR sample returns no defects on tested circuits, but the inspector observes a generic Section D issue (e.g. inadequate labelling on an old distribution board). The defensible action is:

options.A: Code the labelling observation (typically C3) on the EICR and record where it was observed
options.B: Ignore it because the sampled circuits passed

questions.explanation: Visual observations that are outside the sampling scope can still be coded. Inadequate labelling is typically C3 — the inspector records it where seen, and the EICR captures both the test results and the wider observations.

questions.prompt: An EICR limitation reads 'no test results for the lift motor circuit because access denied by the lift maintenance contractor'. This is:

options.A: Defensible, with reason recorded; the inspector recommends a follow-up coordinated with the lift contractor
options.B: Indefensible — the lift must be tested
options.C: Defensible only if the lift is non-passenger
options.D: Defensible only with a fee uplift

questions.explanation: Third-party access restrictions are common limitations. Document the reason and recommend a coordinated follow-up — that protects both parties and gives the duty holder the information to plan the missing inspection.

questions.prompt: Sampling decisions on safety-critical systems (fire alarm, emergency lighting, life safety):

options.B: Default to whatever the duty holder asks

questions.explanation: Safety-critical systems are 100% by default — they fail closed. The consequence of an undetected defect is immediate. Routine sampling rates do not apply to fire alarm and emergency lighting verification.

questions.prompt: Sampling rates may rise for the next cycle when:

options.A: The current EICR turns up multiple defects across several sampling groups
options.B: The current EICR is Satisfactory with no codes
options.D: The duty holder asks for less testing

questions.explanation: Findings drive future sampling. Defects across multiple groups suggest the original sampling rate was too low — the next EICR uses a higher rate (and possibly a shorter interval) until the findings stabilise.

questions.prompt: An EICR records 'inspection limited to non-isolatable items by visual inspection only; full testing where isolation could be agreed during the visit'. This entry is:

options.A: Defensible — visual-only is a recognised limitation, and the items where full testing was possible are clearly distinguished
options.B: Indefensible — visual is never enough

questions.explanation: Visual-only is sometimes the only option (continuous process, no shutdown window). Recording it transparently — and distinguishing the items where full testing was possible — gives the duty holder a clear picture of scope.

questions.prompt: An agreed sampling boundary is exceeded by the inspector during the visit because of findings. The defensible record is:

options.A: Update Section D / sampling notes with the revised scope and sample size, communicate to the duty holder, and proceed with the expanded test set
options.B: Stick with the original sample because it was agreed

questions.explanation: Sampling can grow on findings. The change is communicated and recorded; the duty holder is informed why the original scope no longer fits. Documentation tracks the revised position.

questions.prompt: On a sampled office lighting circuit the inspector finds an exposed live conductor in a damaged accessory. The defensible response is:

options.B: Treat as C1 (immediate danger), make safe (or warn / isolate), notify the duty holder in writing immediately, and expand sampling on related circuits
options.C: Wait until the report is written

questions.explanation: C1 demands immediate action and same-day written notification. After making safe, the inspector continues with an expanded sample because the original defect rate has been understated by even one C1 finding.

questions.prompt: Sampling must NOT be applied to which of the following on a periodic inspection?

options.A: Repeating socket outlets in an office
options.B: Repeating lighting points in a corridor
options.C: The main earthing terminal, earthing conductor and main protective bonding conductors

questions.explanation: MET, earthing conductor and main protective bonding conductors are unique to the installation and central to every protective measure. They are inspected directly; sampling is for repeating distributed accessories.

questions.prompt: An EICR limitation must not:

options.A: Cover access denied by an occupant
options.B: Cover continuous-process areas where isolation is impossible during the visit
options.C: Be used to hide an observed defect or danger
options.D: Be used for high-risk areas where access was unavailable

questions.explanation: Limitations cannot conceal observed danger. Once an inspector has seen a defect, coding is required regardless of any subsequent agreement to omit. The whole point of limitations is to be transparent about scope.

questions.prompt: An EICR records 'sampling 25% of repeating accessories; 100% of consumer units, switchgear, fire alarm circuits and emergency lighting'. This sampling pattern is:

options.A: Defensible — origin/critical 100%, repeating distributed at typical 10-25%
options.B: Indefensible — sampling must be uniform
options.C: Indefensible — fire alarm cannot be tested at all on a periodic

questions.explanation: Mixed sampling is the realistic approach — origin and critical systems 100%, repeating accessories at lower rates. Anything blanket — '100% everywhere' or 'sample everything' — does not reflect actual practice.

questions.prompt: A previous EICR set sampling at 50% and found three defects. The inspector inheriting the next cycle should:

options.A: Sample at 50% again as a baseline, expanding on findings, and consider whether the previous defect rate justifies a higher starting sample or shorter interval
options.B: Sample at 5%

questions.explanation: Previous findings inform the next inspection. The new inspector reviews the previous EICR, sets a starting sample size that reflects the previous defect rate, and adjusts the interval if conditions warrant.

questions.prompt: An EICR sample reveals a low IR reading on a sampled circuit. The cause cannot be diagnosed during the visit without further isolation that the duty holder cannot accommodate today. The defensible response is:

options.A: Issue Unsatisfactory with FI, recording the symptom and the reason further investigation cannot be completed today
options.B: Issue Satisfactory with a footnote

questions.explanation: FI is for symptoms that cannot be diagnosed during the visit. The report is Unsatisfactory until the FI is closed out by a follow-up visit and any consequent remedial work.

questions.prompt: Live testing during a periodic inspection is governed by GS38 in respect of:

options.A: Test lead and probe construction (insulated probes, fused leads, finger guards, exposed tip length)
options.B: Volt drop calculations

questions.explanation: GS38 is HSE guidance on test leads and probes. Insulated probes, fused leads (typically 500mA fuse), finger guards, and limited exposed tip length all aim to keep the inspector safe during live work.

questions.prompt: An EICR sample reveals two non-compliant accessories among the ten sampled. The inspector should:

options.A: Issue Satisfactory because the rate is only 20%
options.B: Code the accessories appropriately, expand the sample to the wider population, and communicate the pattern in the EICR

questions.explanation: 20% defect rate is significant — the sample should expand. Each defect is coded, and the EICR records the pattern and the expanded scope. The overall result depends on the codes raised.

questions.prompt: A duty holder asks 'why isn't 100% always tested?' The defensible response is:

options.B: Practicability — full testing is often not reasonably practicable on large installations; sampling extrapolated from a representative subset is defensible when properly agreed and recorded

questions.explanation: Practicability is the defensible reason. Full testing on a large installation is often not reasonably practicable; sampling — agreed, documented, and risk-based — gives a defensible view at a proportionate scope.

questions.prompt: An EICR limitation is recorded as 'lighting circuits in occupied bedrooms not tested'. The duty holder is comfortable with this. The defensible record is:

options.A: Section D, with reason 'occupant present; no isolation window during the visit', plus the duty holder's signed acceptance
options.B: Verbal note to the duty holder only
options.D: Record on the test results schedule only

questions.explanation: Section D plus signed acceptance is the textbook treatment. The duty holder is left with a clear picture: which areas were not tested, why, and a recommendation to follow up if needed.

questions.prompt: Sampling on a hospital's life-safety circuits should default to:
questions.explanation: Life-safety systems are 100% by default. Routine sampling rates do not apply — the consequence of an undetected defect on emergency lighting or life-safety power is immediate.

questions.prompt: Live test for Zs is being carried out on a TN-S installation while the building is occupied. The most defensible approach is:

options.A: Use loop tester with appropriate test leads (GS38 compliant), wear appropriate PPE, work to the inspector's documented risk assessment, and record the live-test rationale in Section D
options.B: Use loop tester with no PPE for speed
options.C: Use loop tester with the duty holder absent

questions.explanation: GS38 leads + PPE + RA + documented rationale is the textbook live-test setup. Speed and absence of duty holder are not relevant; the live-test exception requires extra controls, not fewer.

questions.prompt: An EICR sample turns up no defects but the inspector observes the consumer unit is plastic and visibly aged. The defensible response is:

options.A: Code as appropriate (typically C3 for non-fire-rated plastic CU in older installations, or further coding if heat-damaged) and note the observation outside the sampling scope
options.B: Ignore because samples passed

questions.explanation: Visual observations sit alongside test sampling. A non-fire-rated plastic consumer unit is typically C3 in older domestic installations; if there is heat damage or melted material the code can rise to C2 or C1.
