questions.prompt: An EICR for a privately rented dwelling has Section D blank. The implication is:

options.A: The report is incomplete and the landlord may not have a defensible record under ESS PRS 2020
options.B: The report is fine because PRS Regs are silent on Section D
options.C: The report is fine because dwellings are simple
options.D: The report is fine because no codes were raised

questions.explanation: ESS PRS 2020 expects a complete EICR. Section D is part of the standard set; its absence undermines the report and weakens the landlord's documentary position with the local authority and tenant.

questions.prompt: An EICR sample returns no defects but the inspector observes that the test results from the previous EICR were significantly different. The defensible response is:

options.A: Investigate the discrepancy, record the comparison in the new EICR, and code or raise FI as appropriate
options.B: Ignore the previous EICR

questions.explanation: Trends matter. A significant change between cycles deserves investigation — it could indicate deterioration, alteration or a previous test error. The new EICR should reflect the inspector's diagnosis.

questions.prompt: On a sampled circuit, the inspector sees an obvious sign of overheating at a connection. The defensible response is:

options.A: Investigate the connection, code appropriately (typically C2 or higher depending on severity), and expand sampling on related accessories of the same type
options.B: Code C3 and stop

questions.explanation: Overheating typically codes C2 (potentially dangerous — risk of fire) or C1 if the danger is immediate. Investigation reveals the cause, expanded sampling tests for the pattern, and the EICR captures the wider position.

questions.prompt: An EICR Section D limitation reads 'isolation refused by duty holder for cost reasons'. This entry is:

options.A: Defensible — duty holder accepts the residual risk in writing
options.B: Indefensible because cost is not a recognised reason for limitation

questions.explanation: The duty holder can choose to accept residual risk in writing for genuine commercial reasons. The inspector's job is to make the position transparent — the limitation, the reason, and the duty holder's signed acceptance.

questions.prompt: An EICR records 'live RCD operation tested at IΔn (built-in button) only; trip-time test deferred to next cycle for non-isolation reasons'. This is:

options.A: A documented limitation: the inspector should record it in Section D and recommend completion at the next opportunity
options.B: A failure to test — Unsatisfactory automatically
options.D: A reason to refer to the DNO

questions.explanation: Partial testing recorded as a limitation is acceptable when the reason is genuine. The duty holder is left with a clear picture: what was tested, what wasn't, and what the next visit needs to complete.

questions.prompt: Sampling on a TT installation:

options.A: Follows the same risk-based principles as for any other earthing system
options.B: Is forbidden

questions.explanation: Earthing system does not change the sampling principle. TT installations follow the same risk-based sampling logic — origin/electrode 100%, repeating accessories at typical 10-20% rates, escalated on findings.

questions.prompt: An EICR limitation that contradicts an observed danger is:

options.A: Defensible if the duty holder agrees
options.B: Indefensible — observed danger must be coded; the limitation route cannot be used to hide it
options.C: Defensible if the customer is in a hurry

questions.explanation: Once danger is observed, coding is required. The limitation route is for items not inspected, not for items inspected and known to be defective. Hiding observed danger is a serious professional failure.

questions.prompt: An inspector samples 10 lighting points on a corridor and finds two with damaged flexes inside accessory boxes. The defensible response is:

options.B: Investigate, code appropriately (typically C2 for damaged flex creating a shock or fire hazard), expand the sample to similar accessories, and record the pattern
options.D: Issue Satisfactory because lighting circuits are low risk

questions.explanation: Damaged flex is a shock and fire hazard — typically C2. The inspector codes each instance, expands the sample to similar accessories, and the EICR captures the pattern.

questions.prompt: An inspector cannot dead-test a hospital's MRI scanner power circuit. The defensible response is:

options.B: Treat as a limitation, agree the limitation in writing with the duty holder, and apply only those tests that can be safely carried out without affecting clinical use
options.C: Issue Unsatisfactory just for the MRI

questions.explanation: Critical clinical equipment cannot be casually isolated. The limitation route — agreed, recorded, with proportionate live tests — is the textbook treatment. The duty holder accepts the residual position in writing.

questions.prompt: Inspecting a privately rented dwelling, the inspector finds the loft hatch sealed shut. The defensible record is:

options.A: Limitation in Section D, with reason 'loft hatch sealed; no access during the visit', recommending follow-up access
options.B: Force entry

questions.explanation: Sealed access is a textbook Section D limitation. Document the reason, recommend a follow-up — the duty holder retains the duty to enable access for periodic inspection.

questions.prompt: A duty holder asks for sampling at 5% to keep the cost down. The defensible response is:

options.B: Discuss the implications with the duty holder, propose a defensible sample (with origin/critical systems at 100%), document the agreed scope in writing, and expand on findings

questions.explanation: The conversation matters. Origin and critical systems stay 100%. Repeating accessories sample at a rate the inspector considers defensible, agreed in writing, and increased on findings — the inspector cannot accept a sample size they consider inadequate.

questions.prompt: The 'reasonably practicable' standard for periodic inspection means:

options.A: Whatever the inspector can finish in a day
options.B: A balance between the risk involved and the time, cost, and effort needed to address it — a recognised legal test from HSWA
options.C: Whatever the duty holder pays for

questions.explanation: Reasonably practicable is the HSWA test. The inspector balances risk against time/cost/effort, but cannot use cost alone to omit testing where the consequence is dangerous.

questions.prompt: On a dead test, an inspector finds a circuit with a low IR reading. The duty holder asks them to skip further investigation because the circuit is in continuous use. The defensible response is:

options.B: Record a limitation explaining the constraint, raise FI for the circuit, and recommend follow-up — the symptom does not disappear because access was denied

questions.explanation: FI is for symptoms that cannot be diagnosed during the visit. The report is Unsatisfactory until FI is closed out. The duty holder is responsible for arranging the follow-up visit.

questions.prompt: An EICR sample reveals a deteriorated PVC sheath. The defensible response is:

options.A: Code the deterioration appropriately (typically C2 if integrity is compromised), expand sampling to similar areas, and record the pattern
options.B: Code C3 and stop

questions.explanation: Deteriorated sheaths code C2 if integrity is compromised. The inspector expands the sample because deterioration usually correlates with location/exposure — similar areas elsewhere likely show the same pattern.

questions.prompt: Live testing introduces additional hazards. The inspector's primary defence is:

options.B: GS38 leads, appropriate PPE, a documented risk assessment, agreed scope, and the duty holder's signed acceptance of residual risk

questions.explanation: The defensible toolkit for live testing: GS38, PPE, RA, documented scope, signed acceptance. Live testing is the documented exception, not the working norm.

questions.prompt: A duty holder asks for sampling to be 'whatever the inspector decides on the day'. The defensible response is:

options.B: Document the agreed sampling approach in writing before the inspection (with origin/critical at 100% and repeating accessories at typical 10-20%), and revise in writing during the visit if conditions change

questions.explanation: Vague verbal agreements give no documentary protection. The defensible approach is a written baseline before the inspection (origin/critical 100%; repeating accessories at typical sample rates), revised in writing during the visit as needed.

questions.prompt: An EICR records 'sampling: 100% of consumer units; 30% of socket outlets, sampled across all rooms in proportion'. This is:

options.A: Defensible — origin 100%, repeating distributed at a rate weighted across the population, with a representative spread
options.B: Indefensible — sampling must be uniform

questions.explanation: Mixed and weighted sampling is normal. Origin 100%, sockets at a rate that gives a representative spread across the population, with the rationale documented. The headline rate is the inspector's risk-based judgement.

questions.prompt: An EICR limitation that says 'tenants in occupation; rooms tested where access permitted' is:

options.A: Defensible — operational limitation, recorded with reason and recommended follow-up
options.B: Indefensible — every room must be tested

questions.explanation: Occupied tenancies are a real-world constraint on access. Recording the limitation with reason and a follow-up recommendation is the textbook treatment; full testing is achieved over multiple visits if needed.

questions.prompt: The inspector observes during the EICR that a previously installed circuit has been altered with no documentation. The defensible response is:

options.A: Investigate, code appropriately (typically FI if the alteration cannot be assessed during the visit; C2 if it creates a potential danger; C3 if compliant but undocumented), and record the observation
options.B: Ignore the alteration

questions.explanation: Undocumented alterations are common and depend on what the inspector finds. The default is investigate; code follows the actual condition. FI is appropriate when the assessment cannot be completed during the visit.

questions.prompt: Sampling failure escalation should NOT be:

options.B: Documented
options.C: Suppressed at the duty holder's request

questions.explanation: Escalation cannot be suppressed by the duty holder. The inspector communicates the change, but the decision to expand sampling on findings is a professional judgement the duty holder cannot override.

questions.prompt: An EICR is a 'snapshot' precisely because:

options.A: It documents the agreed scope only
options.B: It records the condition of the installation on the day of inspection — sampling, limitations, codes raised; future deterioration is the duty holder's responsibility to manage between cycles
options.C: It only counts as evidence on the day it is signed

questions.explanation: Snapshot logic underpins everything: the EICR is current on the day, and the duty holder is responsible for in-service safety between cycles. Sampling, limitations and codes all reflect that day's findings.

questions.prompt: A duty holder asks for the sampled accessories to be selected randomly with no inspector preference. The defensible response is:

options.A: Inspector selects a representative sample using professional judgement, weighting toward high-risk areas, and records the rationale
options.B: Random sampling without weighting
options.D: Test only the duty holder's office

questions.explanation: Sampling is not random — it is risk-based. The inspector weights the sample toward high-risk areas (kitchens, wet rooms, public access) and records the rationale. Random selection ignores the risk profile and is not defensible.

questions.prompt: An EICR limitation reads 'live circuits to clinical alarms not isolated; functional check only by tester'. This is:

options.A: Defensible if reason and method are recorded and the duty holder accepts the residual risk in writing
options.B: Indefensible because clinical alarms must be dead-tested

questions.explanation: Clinical alarms cannot be casually isolated. A documented limitation with functional check, agreed in writing, is a textbook treatment for life-critical equipment that cannot be dead-tested during the visit.

questions.prompt: An EICR records 'sampling of consumer units: 100%; sampling of distribution boards: 100%; sampling of repeating sockets: 15%; lighting: 15%; fire alarm: 100%; emergency lighting: 100%'. The pattern is:

options.A: Defensible — origins/critical 100%, repeating accessories at typical 10-20%
options.B: Indefensible — sampling must be uniform
options.C: Indefensible — fire alarm cannot be sampled

questions.explanation: Mixed sampling that respects the risk profile is exactly what GN3 expects. Origins, distribution and life-safety at 100%; repeating accessories at lower rates that reflect their risk and replication.

questions.prompt: An EICR limitation cannot exclude a circuit where the inspector has already observed:

options.B: Polarity issue

questions.explanation: Once observed, danger must be coded. The limitation route is for un-inspected items, not for items inspected and known to be defective. The inspector cannot exclude an observed defect at the duty holder's request.

questions.prompt: Live RCD trip-time testing on a TT installation in a dwelling:

options.A: Is normally required at the inspection — the test is brief and the consequences of an undetected RCD failure are immediate (TT relies on RCD for fault disconnection)
options.B: Should always be omitted

questions.explanation: TT installations rely on RCDs for ADS. Skipping the trip-time test on TT is rarely defensible — the RCD is the protective device. The check is brief and the consequence of failure is direct.

questions.prompt: An EICR limitation entry should include, as a minimum:

options.A: Item or area, reason, agreed by/with whom, and a recommended follow-up if appropriate
options.B: Just the item

questions.explanation: A complete Section D entry: what was excluded, why, who agreed, and what to do next. Short-form entries miss the documentary point — clarity protects both the inspector and the duty holder.

questions.prompt: You observe cracking and heat damage on the DNO cut-out. No live parts are accessible to the user. How should this normally affect the EICR?

options.A: Code it C2 and make the EICR unsatisfactory because all intake equipment is part of the installation
options.B: Ignore it because distributor equipment is never mentioned on an EICR
options.C: Comment on it, advise urgent contact with the DNO/supplier, but do not let it determine the overall assessment unless it creates accessible live parts or immediate danger
options.D: Record it as N/A with no further action

questions.explanation: Distributor equipment is not normally part of the consumer's installation, but dangerous or damaged intake equipment should be reported and escalated. It does not normally decide the EICR outcome unless it gives access to live parts or creates immediate danger to users.

questions.prompt: During an EICR of a cafe, the client expects the coffee machine, refrigeration units, dishwasher, extract fan, fire alarm panel, emergency lighting, intruder alarm and fixed wiring all to be "covered by the EICR." Which answer is best?

options.A: The EICR automatically certifies all appliances and specialist systems
options.B: The EICR covers only portable appliances, not fixed wiring
options.C: The EICR covers fixed wiring only and must never mention fixed equipment
options.D: The EICR primarily covers the fixed installation and supplies; appliances and specialist systems may require separate inspection/testing regimes unless specifically included

questions.explanation: Fixed wiring, distribution equipment, accessories, isolation and circuit protective measures are the core EICR scope. Appliances, fire alarms, emergency lighting and security systems often need separate specialist inspection and test documentation. The report scope should avoid misleading the client.

questions.prompt: A 2012 domestic plastic consumer unit is under wooden stairs forming the sole escape route. There is no damage, no overheating, no missing blanks, no loose connections and all circuits test satisfactorily. What is the most defensible classification?

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: A combustible/plastic consumer unit in a sole escape route is normally an improvement recommendation where there is no evidence of thermal damage or other defects. It could become C2 if overheating, loose terminations, damaged enclosure, poor entries or increased fire-spread risk are present. Accessible live parts would be C1.

questions.prompt: A spare way in a consumer unit has a missing blank. With the cover fitted, a child could insert a finger or thin object and contact live parts. What is the correct classification?

options.B: C2
options.D: No reportable observation because covers are not part of the electrical installation

questions.explanation: If live parts are accessible to ordinary persons in normal use, immediate danger is present. The defect should be made safe immediately. The answer may differ where live parts are exposed only after a tool-required cover is removed by a skilled person, but that is not this scenario.

questions.prompt: An EICR records 'Satisfactory'. This means:

options.A: The installation is fully compliant with the current edition with no observations
options.B: No C1, C2 or FI observations were raised; the installation is safe for continued use, with any C3 items recommended for improvement
options.C: The installation has been certified for new use
options.D: The installation has had remedial work completed

questions.explanation: Satisfactory means no C1, C2 or FI. C3 items can be present and the report is still Satisfactory. The duty holder reviews C3 observations as improvement opportunities, but the installation is safe for continued use.

questions.prompt: An EICR records 'Unsatisfactory'. This means:

options.B: At least one C1, C2 or FI observation was raised; remedial action and/or further investigation is required to make the report Satisfactory
options.C: The next inspection is due immediately

questions.explanation: Unsatisfactory means at least one C1, C2 or FI. Remedial action (and follow-up confirmation) is required. The installation continues in use only with the dangerous items addressed and recorded.

questions.prompt: Periodic test sequences differ from initial verification because:

options.B: The installation is already energised and in service; the inspector applies appropriate tests using sampling and judgement, guided by GN3, rather than the prescribed initial-verification sequence

questions.explanation: Periodic inspection happens on a live, in-use installation. The dead-test sequence used at initial verification can't always be applied — the inspector picks appropriate tests using sampling and judgement, guided by GN3.

questions.prompt: An EICR identifies an RCD that does not operate when the test button is pressed. This is typically coded:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: An RCD that fails its built-in mechanical test has unproven protection. Typically C2 (potentially dangerous — protection cannot be relied on). On a TT installation where the RCD is the primary fault protection, this can rise to C1.

questions.prompt: An EICR identifies a missing CPC on a final circuit feeding a Class I appliance. The typical code is:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Missing CPC on a Class I circuit removes the protective measure for ADS — typically C2. Where exposed-conductive-parts of the appliance are accessible without barrier, the code can rise to C1.

questions.prompt: An EICR identifies a borrowed neutral between two circuits. The typical code is:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Borrowed neutrals are typically C2 (potentially dangerous — isolation of one circuit leaves a live neutral connection accessible elsewhere). The risk to anyone working on the apparently isolated circuit is significant.

questions.prompt: An EICR identifies a circuit running through a bedroom that has been over-extended such that the inspector suspects but cannot confirm a code-worthy issue without further isolation. The typical code is:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Suspect but unproven, requiring more work — FI. The report is Unsatisfactory until the FI is closed out and a code can be assigned (or removed).

questions.prompt: An EICR observation that 'covers were missing from a junction box, exposing live conductors' is typically coded:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Exposed live conductor is direct contact danger — C1. The inspector should make safe immediately (refit cover, isolate, secure) and notify the duty holder same-day in writing.

questions.prompt: An EICR observation that 'the consumer unit is plastic, in an older domestic installation, with no signs of heat damage' is typically coded:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Plastic CU with no heat damage in an older domestic installation is typically C3 (improvement recommended — non-fire-rated enclosure on the escape route). Signs of heat damage push the code to C2 or C1 depending on severity.

questions.prompt: Periodic inspection in privately rented dwellings is governed by:

options.B: ESS PRS Regulations 2020 (England) — 5-yearly max, supply within 28 days, remedial within 28 days for C1/C2/FI, local authority enforcement

questions.explanation: ESS PRS 2020 is the regime for privately rented dwellings in England. The 5-year max, the 28-day supply duty, the 28-day remedial duty and local-authority enforcement are the headline points.

questions.prompt: An EICR with a C1 must be communicated to the duty holder:

options.B: Immediately and in writing — typically a same-day Danger Notification handed over before the inspector leaves site
options.C: Only if remedial work is needed

questions.explanation: C1 = immediate communication. BPG4 requires the inspector to make safe and notify the duty holder same-day in writing. Waiting until the formal report leaves the duty holder unaware while danger remains.

questions.prompt: An EICR records 'no covers on a junction box; conductor stripped back exposing copper, in a public corridor'. Typical code:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Exposed live conductor in a public corridor is direct contact danger — C1. Public access removes any mitigation by 'restricted to skilled persons'.

questions.prompt: An EICR observation that 'no RCD protects sockets that may reasonably be used to supply outdoor equipment, on an installation in a domestic dwelling' is typically coded:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Missing RCD on sockets likely to feed outdoor equipment is potentially dangerous (BS 7671 Reg 411.3.3) — typically C2. The code recognises that the exposed-to-outdoor risk is real.

questions.prompt: An EICR observation that 'no main protective bonding to a metallic gas pipe at the point of entry' is typically coded:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Missing main bonding is potentially dangerous — exposed metal could rise to fault potential. C2. C1 if there is also evidence of the absence creating immediate danger (e.g. broken neutral on TN-C-S).

questions.prompt: An EICR cover letter exists primarily to:

options.B: Translate the formal report into plain language, summarise the codes and recommended actions, and set out timescales — without changing the technical content
options.C: Allow the duty holder to argue the codes
options.D: Be filed instead of the report

questions.explanation: EICRs are technical. The cover letter is the plain-English bridge — what the codes mean, what to do, when to do it. It complements the report; it doesn't replace it.

questions.prompt: Periodic inspection is required because faults can develop in service that initial verification cannot anticipate. The legal foundation in the workplace is:

options.B: EAWR 1989 Reg 4(2) — duty to maintain so as to prevent danger

questions.explanation: EAWR Reg 4(2) is the duty. Periodic inspection is the recognised technical means of demonstrating compliance, and BS 7671 / GN3 provide the standards and intervals.

questions.prompt: An EICR identifies a permanent missing label on the consumer unit (no circuit ID). Typical code:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Missing labelling alone is C3 (improvement recommended) — the installation works, but identifying and isolating circuits is harder than it should be. Improvement, not danger.

questions.prompt: An EICR identifies a Type AC RCD on a circuit feeding equipment that produces DC fault current (e.g. an EV charger or an inverter). The typical code is:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Type AC RCDs cannot reliably trip on DC residual current. On circuits with electronic loads producing DC fault current, the protection is unproven — typically C2 (potentially dangerous). The current edition requires Type A or above.

questions.prompt: An EICR observation that 'the disconnection time on a TN-S final circuit cannot be met because the measured Zs is significantly above the table value' is typically coded:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Disconnection time not met is potentially dangerous — fault current may persist long enough to cause shock or damage. Typically C2; C1 if the consequences are immediate (e.g. very high Zs or accessible exposed-conductive-parts on a public route).

questions.prompt: An EICR's Schedule of Test Results captures:

options.B: The actual measured values (Zs, R1+R2, IR, RCD trip times, etc.) for each circuit tested, plus the inspector's assessment of those values

questions.explanation: The Schedule of Test Results is the documentary evidence behind the codes — the actual measurements per circuit. Without it, the codes have no defensible basis and the report is incomplete.

questions.prompt: BPG4 is published by the IET and gives:

options.B: A list of typical EICR observations and the recommended C1/C2/C3/FI code for each

questions.explanation: BPG4 is the standard reference for EICR coding. When an inspector is unsure how to code an observation, BPG4's typical-coding lists are the recognised industry baseline.

questions.prompt: An EICR observation that 'no main protective bonding to incoming metallic water pipe' is typically coded:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Missing main bonding is potentially dangerous — typically C2. The exposed pipework could rise to fault potential, and any persons in contact with both the pipe and earth could be exposed.

questions.prompt: The 28-day clock under ESS PRS Regs 2020 starts from:

options.B: The date the report is supplied to the existing tenant — landlord must supply within 28 days of the EICR
options.C: The date the local authority requests the report
options.D: The date a tenant moves in

questions.explanation: ESS PRS 2020: existing tenants get the EICR within 28 days of the inspection. The clock for that supply duty starts at the EICR date itself, not at any later trigger.

questions.prompt: An EICR Unsatisfactory result on a privately rented dwelling triggers a 28-day duty to:

options.B: Complete remedial work for any C1/C2/FI and provide written confirmation to the tenant and to the local authority on request

questions.explanation: ESS PRS 2020: 28-day remedial duty (or sooner if the inspector specifies). Written confirmation goes to the tenant and to the local authority on request. Re-testing is not the statutory step; remedial work and confirmation are.

questions.prompt: An inspector finds a C1. They must, in priority order:

options.A: Make safe (or warn / isolate) immediately, notify the duty holder in writing same day, then complete the formal report
options.B: Wait until the formal report
options.D: Refer to the DNO and leave

questions.explanation: C1 is immediate. Make safe first; notify the duty holder same-day in writing; complete the formal report afterwards. The order matters — danger is removed before paperwork is finalised.

questions.prompt: An EICR Schedule of Inspections lists items that have been:

options.B: Visually inspected against the BS 7671 / Schedule of Inspection items

questions.explanation: Schedule of Inspections covers what was looked at — visual checks against the standard items (cable connections, IDs, identifications, signs of damage, etc.). Tests with measured values go on the Schedule of Test Results.

questions.prompt: An EICR identifies a final circuit where measured Zs is 1.3 Ω, BS 7671 tabulated maximum is 1.37 Ω. Applying the GN3 80% rule of thumb the result is:

options.A: Pass — the measured value is below the table value
options.B: Borderline / fail under the rule of thumb — 80% of 1.37 Ω is approximately 1.10 Ω, and 1.3 Ω is above that limit
options.C: Fail because Zs is never measurable

questions.explanation: GN3 rule of thumb: measured cold Zs should be no more than 80% of the table value to allow for conductor heating. 1.37 × 0.8 = 1.096 Ω. A reading of 1.3 Ω fails the rule of thumb and should be investigated, not waved through.

questions.prompt: Test sequences for periodic inspection are:

options.B: Selected by the inspector using GN3 as guidance and the installation's risk profile as the driver — judgement-led, not prescribed

questions.explanation: Unlike initial verification, periodic doesn't have a prescribed test sequence. The inspector selects the appropriate tests using GN3 and the risk profile, applying sampling where appropriate and live testing only where dead testing isn't practicable.

questions.prompt: A C2 made the EICR Unsatisfactory. The duty holder under EAWR has to:

options.A: Take reasonable action to remove the danger as soon as practicable
options.B: Wait until the next inspection cycle
options.D: Disregard the C2 because it is not a C1

questions.explanation: C2 = potentially dangerous and must be acted on. EAWR's duty to maintain so as to prevent danger applies — the action must be reasonable, proportionate and timely, and the report Unsatisfactory until resolved.

questions.prompt: A privately rented dwelling EICR is Unsatisfactory due to FI. Under ESS PRS 2020 the landlord must:

options.A: Wait for the report to be reissued without action
options.B: Arrange the further investigation, complete any consequent remedial work, and obtain written confirmation within 28 days (or sooner if the inspector specifies)

questions.explanation: FI also makes the report Unsatisfactory under ESS PRS. The landlord must arrange the further investigation and any consequent remedial work within 28 days, with written confirmation.

questions.prompt: An EICR identifies an old porcelain fuse-carrier consumer unit with no overload protection and no RCDs in a privately rented dwelling. The inspector should code this:

options.B: Typically C2 (potentially dangerous — significantly below current standards), with possible escalation to C1 if there are signs of overload or damage

questions.explanation: Old consumer units without modern protection are typically C2 — significantly below current standards, no RCD protection where now required. Escalation to C1 follows specific evidence (heat damage, exposed live, etc.).

questions.prompt: An EICR finds a damaged fixed accessory cover that is no longer locked or secured. Typical code:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Damaged cover that no longer keeps live parts behind a barrier is typically C2 (potentially dangerous — direct contact possible if the cover moves). Where the cover is missing entirely and live parts are exposed, the code rises to C1.

questions.prompt: An EICR observation that 'main bonding conductors are sized 6 mm² where 10 mm² is required for the supply' is typically coded:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Undersized main bonding fails to provide the required equipotential at fault — typically C2 (potentially dangerous). Where the consequences become immediate (e.g. broken PEN on TN-C-S), the code rises to C1.

questions.prompt: A privately rented dwelling EICR identifies one C2. The landlord arranges remedial work within 28 days. The follow-up document is:

options.B: Written confirmation that the remedial work has been completed (typically a Minor Works Certificate or a letter from the contractor) supplied to the tenant and to the local authority on request
options.D: An EIC for the whole installation

questions.explanation: ESS PRS 2020 expects written confirmation of remedial completion. A MEIWC for the work or a contractor letter confirming the remedial action and any retest results is the typical document.

questions.prompt: An EICR Schedule of Test Results columns typically include:

options.B: Circuit identification, conductor sizes, RCD type, R1+R2, IR (L-N, L-E, N-E), Zs measured, RCD trip times, polarity check

questions.explanation: Full Schedule of Test Results captures circuit ID, conductors, protective device, RCD details, all measured values, plus the polarity check. Without that, the report cannot defend its codes.

questions.prompt: An EICR is dated and signed. The signing inspector must:

options.B: Be a competent person who has personally carried out (or directly supervised and verified) the inspection and testing

questions.explanation: Competent person who has carried out (or supervised and verified) the work signs the report. Sign-off is a personal professional act — the signer is accountable for the codes raised.

questions.prompt: An EICR identifies a circuit feeding a sauna where the IP rating of the accessories is below the requirement for the special location zone. Typical code:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Wrong IP rating in a special location is typically C2 (potentially dangerous — water/steam ingress can lead to insulation breakdown). The location-specific zoning is intended to manage that risk; failure to meet it is significant.

questions.prompt: An EICR is signed Unsatisfactory but the duty holder asks for it to be re-issued as Satisfactory once remedial work is complete. The defensible response is:

options.A: Re-issue as Satisfactory after the remedial work
options.B: The original EICR records condition at the time of inspection and is not amended retrospectively. A new follow-up report or certificate covers the remedial work; the original is archived

questions.explanation: Snapshot principle. The original EICR stands as a record of the day. Remedial work is documented separately — typically a follow-up EICR or a MEIWC for the specific repairs.

questions.prompt: A landlord under ESS PRS 2020 fails to commission an EICR. The local authority can:

options.B: Require the landlord to act, take remedial action themselves and recover costs, and impose a financial penalty up to £30,000 per breach

questions.explanation: Local authority enforcement is significant. They can require action, do the work themselves and recover costs, and impose financial penalties up to £30,000 per breach. Multiple breaches stack.

questions.prompt: An EICR is Satisfactory but contains five C3 observations. The duty holder is:

options.A: Required to action all C3 observations within 28 days
options.B: Encouraged to consider the C3 observations but is not legally compelled to act on them — the report is Satisfactory regardless
options.C: Required to commission a new EICR
options.D: Required to switch off the installation

questions.explanation: C3 = improvement recommended. The report is Satisfactory. The duty holder may schedule the C3 work as part of routine maintenance, but there is no statutory deadline as there is for C1/C2/FI.

questions.prompt: An EICR observation that 'no SPD on a domestic installation in a low-risk area' is typically coded:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Missing SPD where current rules now require one, on an older installation that is otherwise compliant, is typically C3 (improvement recommended). It is a departure from the current edition but does not in itself create a danger.

questions.prompt: An EICR observation that 'an exposed conductive part is not connected to the CPC' is typically coded:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Unbonded exposed conductive part removes the protective measure for ADS — typically C2. Where the part is on a public route or in a wet area, the code can escalate to C1.

questions.prompt: Periodic inspection of construction-site temporary supplies is typically required at intervals of:

options.B: 1 year

questions.explanation: GN3 typically gives 3 months for construction-site installations. The combination of mechanical abuse, weather and continuous reconfiguration drives the short interval.

questions.prompt: An EICR observation that 'a circuit has no main earth at the consumer unit' is typically coded:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Missing main earth means the protective measure is non-functional — fault disconnection cannot be assured. Typically C1. The inspector should make safe (typically isolate the affected installation) and notify the duty holder same-day in writing.

questions.prompt: An EICR identifies a missing CPC at a metallic accessory. The typical code is:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Missing CPC at a metallic accessory removes the protective measure — typically C2. Escalation to C1 follows where the accessory is exposed to direct touch and could rise to fault potential.

questions.prompt: An EICR identifies a non-RCD-protected socket outlet in a privately rented dwelling that may reasonably be used for outdoor equipment. The typical code is:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Missing RCD on a likely-outdoor-feed socket is potentially dangerous (Reg 411.3.3) — typically C2. The current edition requires RCD protection; the older installation's failure to comply on this kind of socket is significant.

questions.prompt: An EICR cover letter, when used, is most effective when it:

options.B: Translates the codes into plain English, summarises action and timescales, and complements (does not replace) the formal report

questions.explanation: The cover letter is the bridge between the technical EICR and the duty holder's understanding. Plain English, action items, timescales — it complements the formal report without changing its codes.

questions.prompt: EICR codes derive from the IET BPG4 — they are:

options.B: Industry-recognised guidance that gives a consistent basis for coding observations across inspectors

questions.explanation: BPG4 codes are guidance, but they are the recognised industry standard. Using them gives the duty holder a coding framework that any subsequent inspector can interpret consistently.

questions.prompt: An EICR can use 'NA' (not applicable) or 'LIM' (limitation) instead of a code where:

options.A: The inspector wants to skip the test
options.B: The item does not apply to the installation (NA) or the item could not be inspected within the agreed scope (LIM, with reason)

questions.explanation: NA where genuinely not applicable; LIM where outside the agreed scope (with reason in Section D). Both are legitimate alternatives to a code. Neither is a way to skip an item the inspector should have looked at.

questions.prompt: An EICR is signed by:

options.B: The competent person who has carried out (or directly supervised and verified) the inspection and testing

questions.explanation: Competent person who carried out the work signs. The duty holder typically counter-signs to confirm receipt and acceptance of any extent and limitations, but the inspection responsibility is the inspector's.

questions.prompt: An EICR identifies a CPC connected to a Class II appliance terminal. The typical code is:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: CPC at a Class II appliance terminal is a workmanship issue, not in itself a danger — Class II equipment is double-insulated and the CPC has no functional role. Typically C3 (improvement recommended) — remove or isolate the CPC at the accessory.

questions.prompt: An EICR identifies an installation that is wired to the 15th edition (pre-1992) cable colours. The typical code is:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Old cable colours alone are not dangerous — C3 (improvement recommended). The installation is sound; the colours just don't match current convention. A clear warning notice at the consumer unit is usually all that is needed.

questions.prompt: An EICR identifies a dual-supply installation where the changeover does not fully break each supply (i.e. the two supplies could be paralleled). Typical code:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: A changeover that allows the two supplies to be paralleled is potentially dangerous — fault levels and protection coordination cannot be guaranteed. Typically C2; can rise to C1 if the consequences are immediate.

questions.prompt: An EICR identifies an RCD with the wrong rated residual current (e.g. 100 mA where 30 mA is required). Typical code:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Wrong rated residual current means the additional protection (typically required at 30 mA for human safety) is not provided — typically C2. C1 if the missing protection on a circuit creates an immediate danger (e.g. socket-outlets in a special location).

questions.prompt: An EICR identifies a TN-C-S installation where there is no main protective bonding to the gas service. Typical code:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Missing main bonding on TN-C-S is potentially dangerous — typically C2. Where there is evidence of broken PEN, missing earth at the origin or other immediate danger, the code rises to C1.

questions.prompt: An EICR observation that 'an installation does not meet current Section 715 IP rating requirements for an outdoor location' is typically coded:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Wrong IP rating in an outdoor location risks moisture ingress and insulation breakdown — typically C2. Direct evidence of damage / live parts exposed pushes the code to C1.

questions.prompt: Periodic inspection's place in the maintenance lifecycle is best described as:

options.B: A condition-assessment that informs the duty holder's wider maintenance and risk-management decisions, supporting EAWR compliance

questions.explanation: PIT is a condition-assessment exercise. It feeds into the duty holder's wider maintenance, replacement and risk-management decisions and is the recognised means of demonstrating EAWR compliance.

questions.prompt: An EICR identifies a plastic consumer unit on a TN-C-S domestic installation, with signs of localised heat damage at one of the breakers. Typical code:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Heat damage in the consumer unit is potentially dangerous — typically C2 (risk of fire). Where the damage is severe or there is evidence of breaker malfunction, the code escalates to C1.

questions.prompt: An EICR identifies a sub-main where the protective conductor has not been adequately sized for fault current. Typical code:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Undersized protective conductor on a sub-main risks failure to disconnect fault current safely — typically C2. C1 follows where the consequences are immediate (very large under-sizing or evidence of damage).

questions.prompt: An EICR's overall assessment is determined by:

options.A: The total number of codes raised
options.B: Whether any C1, C2 or FI is present (Unsatisfactory) — C3 alone is Satisfactory regardless of count
options.C: The total cost of remedial work

questions.explanation: Pass/fail of the overall assessment is binary on C1/C2/FI. C3 has no effect on the overall result regardless of how many are listed; only C1/C2/FI move the report to Unsatisfactory.

questions.prompt: The scope of Building Regulations Part P (England) is restricted to:

options.B: Notifiable electrical work carried out in dwellings

questions.explanation: Part P is a Building Regulations duty covering notifiable electrical work in dwellings (England). It controls new and altered work in domestic premises but does not directly govern periodic inspection.

questions.prompt: ESS PRS 2020 financial penalty per breach can reach:
questions.explanation: Local authorities can impose penalties up to £30,000 per breach. Multiple breaches stack — failure to commission an EICR, failure to supply within timescales, failure to act on C1/C2/FI within 28 days.

questions.prompt: The Schedule of Test Results that accompanies an EICR is intended to record:

options.B: Per-circuit measurements (R1+R2, IR, Zs, RCD trip times) and the inspector's assessment of those values

questions.explanation: Per-circuit measured values are the documentary basis for the codes. Without the Schedule of Test Results, the EICR has no defensible foundation for its conclusions.

questions.prompt: An EICR identifies an old metal-clad consumer unit in a domestic kitchen with no signs of damage. Typical code:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Old metal-clad CU with no damage is typically C3 (improvement recommended) — the kitchen environment is a candidate for upgraded protection (RCDs, AFDDs in current edition), but the installation is not in itself dangerous.

questions.prompt: An EICR identifies an unswitched live socket in a public corridor, where the cover has been removed and the live conductor is accessible. Typical code:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Exposed live conductor on a public corridor is direct contact danger — C1. The inspector should make safe (refit/secure or isolate) immediately and notify the duty holder same-day in writing.

questions.prompt: An EICR identifies a final circuit feeding a bathroom that has no supplementary equipotential bonding and no RCD. Typical code:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Bathroom with no RCD and no supplementary bonding is potentially dangerous — typically C2. The current edition relies on 30 mA RCD protection in special locations; the absence is significant. C1 if there is evidence of damaged exposed-conductive-parts that could rise to fault potential.

questions.prompt: An EICR cover letter is typically used to:

options.B: Translate codes and observations into plain language and recommend action and timescales

questions.explanation: Cover letters complement the formal report by giving the duty holder a plain-English summary of the codes, recommended actions, and timescales. They do not replace the technical EICR.

questions.prompt: An EICR observation that 'one circuit has been altered with non-compliant cable colours; otherwise satisfactory' is typically coded:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Altered colours alone are not dangerous — C3 (improvement recommended). A warning notice at the consumer unit and identification at the affected accessory is what is needed; the wiring continues to function safely.

questions.prompt: Periodic inspection in agricultural premises is governed primarily by:

options.B: EAWR 1989 and HSWA 1974, with BS 7671 / GN3 as the recognised technical means

questions.explanation: Agricultural premises are workplaces — EAWR + HSWA apply. BS 7671 / GN3 provide the standards and the typical 3-year interval. ESS PRS is residential-tenancy specific; Part P is dwellings; RIDDOR is incident reporting.

questions.prompt: Periodic test sequences for an in-service installation are:

options.A: Mandated by BS 7671 to follow the initial-verification sequence
options.B: Selected by the inspector using GN3 as guidance and the installation's risk profile as the driver — judgement-led, with appropriate tests applied where dead testing is practicable

questions.explanation: Periodic is judgement-led; initial verification is prescribed. The inspector chooses appropriate tests, samples where reasonable, dead-tests by default, and live-tests as the documented exception.

questions.prompt: An EICR identifies a missing earth electrode on a TT installation. Typical code:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: TT installation without an earth electrode means there is no fault path. Typically C1 (immediate danger — fault disconnection cannot occur). The inspector should make safe (typically isolate the affected installation) and notify the duty holder immediately.

questions.prompt: An EICR observation that 'no warning notice for non-standard cable colours at the consumer unit' is typically coded:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Missing warning notice alone is C3 (improvement recommended). The installation works, but a future inspector or tradesperson needs to be alerted that mixed colours are present. A simple notice fixes it.

questions.prompt: An EICR identifies an underrated supply cable that has been overloaded for the connected demand. Typical code:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Overloaded cable on a real-world basis is potentially dangerous — typically C2 (risk of insulation breakdown and fire). C1 follows when there is evidence of immediate damage (charring, severe heating).

questions.prompt: An EICR identifies a circuit where the protective device has been replaced with a higher rating without checking conductor capacity. Typical code:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Oversized protection means the cable can be overloaded without the device tripping — potentially dangerous (C2). Where there is evidence the cable is already damaged or has been overloaded historically, the code can rise to C1.

questions.prompt: Periodic inspection of a swimming pool plant room finds an unbonded metallic enclosure. Typical code:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Unbonded metallic enclosure in a special location is typically C2 — the supplementary equipotential is the protective layer of the pool's safety strategy. C1 follows where direct evidence shows the enclosure has risen to fault potential.

questions.prompt: An EICR observation that 'the duty holder has not provided documentation of past inspections' is typically coded:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Missing documentation alone is C3 (improvement recommended) — the duty holder's record-keeping has gaps, but the installation may be safe. The inspector recommends starting fresh and keeping records from this EICR forward.

questions.prompt: An EICR identifies a 17th edition installation in a building used as offices. The 18th edition is current. The departures from the 18th are typically coded:

options.B: Each departure is individually assessed; many are typically C3 (improvement recommended) where the departure does not in itself create danger, with C1/C2 reserved for actual safety issues

questions.explanation: Edition departures are not automatically dangerous. Each is individually assessed against actual condition and consequence. Many become C3 (improvement); a smaller number become C2 or C1 where the gap creates a current-day danger.

questions.prompt: An EICR is Unsatisfactory due to one C2. The duty holder asks the inspector to remove the C2 because they will fix it tomorrow. The defensible response is:

options.B: Refuse — the EICR records condition at the time of inspection. A follow-up document (typically a MEIWC for the remedial work) records the subsequent fix
options.C: Issue Unsatisfactory but add a verbal note

questions.explanation: Snapshot principle. The EICR records what was found on the day. Subsequent remedial work is captured by a separate document. The original EICR is archived as the historical record; it is not amended retrospectively.

questions.prompt: An EICR identifies a privately rented dwelling with one C1 (immediate danger) and three C3s. Under ESS PRS 2020 the landlord must:

options.A: Action the C1 within 28 days (or sooner if specified) and supply written confirmation; consider but is not legally compelled to action the C3s
options.B: Action everything in 28 days

questions.explanation: ESS PRS 2020: 28-day duty applies to C1, C2 and FI. C3 is not a statutory deadline — the duty holder reviews these as improvements. The C1 has the same-day inspector duty (notification in writing) on top of the 28-day landlord duty.

questions.prompt: The output of a periodic inspection is fundamentally:

options.B: A documented, defensible condition assessment of the installation as it stood on the day of inspection — the EICR with its schedules, codes, and limitations

questions.explanation: The EICR is a documented, defensible snapshot. It records what was inspected, what was tested, what was found, and what could not be reached — and the duty holder's responsibility to act on the codes and to manage in-service safety thereafter.

questions.prompt: A standard 13 A socket-outlet is installed in a large bathroom, 3.2 m horizontally from the edge of the bath. The circuit has 30 mA RCD protection and tests satisfactorily. What is the best classification?

options.A: C1 because all bathroom sockets are immediately dangerous
options.B: C2 because all bathroom sockets are prohibited regardless of distance
options.C: C3 because RCD protection is present but bathrooms are special locations
options.D: No reportable observation, assuming the measured position is outside the prohibited distance/zones and other external influences are suitable

questions.explanation: A bathroom socket is not automatically a defect. The key issue is its location relative to zones/prohibited distances, RCD protection and suitability for external influences. On the facts given, it is outside the usual 2.5 m restriction from the boundary of Zone 1 and is RCD protected.

questions.prompt: A bathroom has metallic water and heating pipework, Class I equipment, no visible supplementary bonding and no RCD protection to the lighting circuit. Main bonding is present and Zs/disconnection values are satisfactory. If the conditions for omitting supplementary bonding are not met, what is the likely classification?

options.A: No code because main bonding is always enough
options.B: C3 only, because supplementary bonding is old-fashioned
options.D: N/A because bathrooms are excluded from EICRs

questions.explanation: Absence of supplementary bonding where it is required in a bath or shower location is normally C2. Before coding, verify whether all conditions for omission are satisfied, including RCD protection to relevant circuits, verified main bonding and effective connection of exposed- and extraneous-conductive-parts.

questions.prompt: A 2005 lighting circuit has twin-and-earth cables concealed less than 50 mm deep in plasterboard walls. No RCD protection is provided. There is no damage and the circuit tests satisfactorily. What is the normal classification?

options.B: C2 in all cases
options.D: N/A because lighting circuits do not require inspection

questions.explanation: Lack of RCD protection for concealed cables less than 50 mm deep is usually C3 where the cables are otherwise safe, in zones or suitably routed, and there is no evidence of damage. It could become more serious if cables are outside prescribed zones, damaged, in metallic partitions, or there is no effective CPC/fault protection.

questions.prompt: A rural TT installation still uses a voltage-operated earth-leakage circuit breaker as the main protective device. No reliable disconnection test can be made for it, and no 30 mA RCD protection is provided for socket-outlets. What is the best classification approach?

options.A: Likely C2, or FI only if immediate verification is required before confirming; the device cannot be assumed reliable for modern TT fault protection
options.B: No code because the installation appears to have worked for years
options.C: C3 only because voltage-operated ELCBs are always acceptable if old
options.D: N/A because TT installations are outside BS 7671

questions.explanation: Voltage-operated ELCBs can be defeated by parallel paths, bonding changes, reference electrode issues and installation alterations. On a TT installation, fault protection normally relies on effective RCD operation. If this cannot be verified and there is no effective alternative, the risk is potentially dangerous.

questions.prompt: On a ring final circuit test, R1+R2 readings at three sockets read 0.5 Ω, 0.5 Ω and 1.2 Ω. The 1.2 Ω socket is most likely:

options.B: Spurred from the ring (lone spur)

questions.explanation: Spurred sockets read approximately double the in-ring R1+R2 because current goes through 2.5 mm² in one direction (not parallel paths). 1.2 vs 0.5 is roughly the ratio expected for a single spur. Spur-off-spur reads even higher.

questions.prompt: An RCD trip-time test at 1× IΔn on a general-type RCD to BS EN 61008. Maximum allowable time:

options.B: 150 ms

questions.explanation: BS EN 61008 general-type RCD: 300 ms at 1× IΔn, 40 ms at 5× IΔn. The 40 ms figure is the popular memory but applies at the 5× test, not the 1× test.

questions.prompt: A polarity check at a socket reads OK on the test instrument. The defensible interpretation is:

options.A: L is at the L terminal, N is at the N terminal — polarity correct
options.B: Polarity is irrelevant once installed
options.C: Reversed polarity always on cleared circuits
options.D: Polarity is only tested at the consumer unit

questions.explanation: Polarity check confirms L is at the L terminal and N is at the N terminal. Reversed polarity is a fault — typically C2 because protective devices are not in the L conductor and the user can be exposed to live N pin.

questions.prompt: An IR test result on a 230 V final circuit reads 1.5 MΩ. The defensible response is:

options.B: Investigate further — values close to the minimum may indicate developing faults; record observation

questions.explanation: 1.5 MΩ is technically above the 1 MΩ pass threshold but is suspiciously close. GN3 recommends investigation of values close to the limit — they often indicate the start of insulation degradation.

questions.prompt: The dead-test sequence used at initial verification is:

options.A: Continuity of CPCs and bonding, ring continuity, IR, polarity
options.B: IR, polarity, ring continuity, continuity of CPCs
options.D: Variable — there is no recognised sequence

questions.explanation: Initial verification dead-test sequence (BS 7671 Section 64) — continuity of CPCs and bonding, ring continuity, IR, polarity. The sequence is prescribed for initial; for periodic it is not — the inspector chooses appropriate tests using GN3 guidance.

questions.prompt: An EICR identifies a Type AC RCD on a circuit feeding an EV charger. The typical code is:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Type AC RCDs cannot reliably trip on DC residual current. EV chargers can produce DC fault current; the protection is unproven — typically C2 (potentially dangerous). Type A or above is required for these loads in current edition.

questions.prompt: An installation has been altered by adding a new circuit. Documentation for the altered work is:

options.A: Recorded on the EICR cover letter only
options.B: An EIC (or MEIWC if minor) for the altered work, separately from any EICR
options.C: Just an annotation on the test results schedule

questions.explanation: New work and additions are certified by EIC (or MEIWC for minor work). The EICR is for periodic condition assessment of existing in-service work — alterations have their own document.

questions.prompt: An R1+R2 measurement reads 1.2 Ω on a circuit. Calculated cold Zs is approximately:

options.A: Ze + 1.2 Ω, where Ze is the supply impedance
options.B: 1.2 Ω alone

questions.explanation: Zs = Ze + (R1+R2). The cold value is then corrected upward (typically by the GN3 80% rule of thumb against the table value) to allow for conductor heating in service.

questions.prompt: An EICR has multiple departures from the current edition. The defensible action is:

options.B: Code each departure individually with reasoning, against actual condition and consequence

questions.explanation: Each departure is individually assessed. Some become C3 (improvement), others C2 (potentially dangerous), others stay as Satisfactory observations. The EICR should reflect the actual condition and risk, item by item.

questions.prompt: The inspector finds a TN-C-S installation where the gas service has lost its main bonding due to recent gas-meter work. Typical code:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Missing main bonding on TN-C-S is potentially dangerous (C2) — risk of metallic services rising to fault potential, particularly in a broken-PEN scenario. The code escalates to C1 if there is also evidence of broken PEN or other immediate danger.

questions.prompt: A 32 A Type B circuit measures Zs = 1.10 Ω cold. Tabulated maximum is 1.37 Ω. Applying the GN3 80% rule of thumb:

options.B: On the limit — 80% of 1.37 Ω is 1.096 Ω; the reading should be investigated and not waved through

questions.explanation: GN3 rule of thumb: measured cold Zs ≤ 80% of table value. 1.37 × 0.8 = 1.096 Ω. A reading of 1.10 Ω is right on the limit and should be investigated — temperature correction, conductor sizing and fault path all warrant a closer look.

questions.prompt: A periodic inspection is interrupted by a local power cut. The inspector should:

options.B: Stop testing, ensure the affected installations are safe to re-energise when power returns, and record the interruption in the EICR

questions.explanation: Power interruptions during testing complicate results. The inspector pauses, ensures safe re-energisation, and notes the interruption — partial results from before the cut may need re-doing depending on what was being tested.

questions.prompt: The supply impedance Ze on a domestic TN-C-S installation is typically:
questions.explanation: TN-C-S supply impedance Ze is typically a fraction of an Ohm. Distributors quote a maximum (often 0.35 Ω at the cut-out) but actual values are often lower. TT installations typically have much higher Ze due to electrode resistance.

questions.prompt: Periodic inspection of an installation that has been modified without records — the inspector should:

options.B: Investigate, document the as-found state, code as appropriate (C2/C3/FI depending on findings) and recommend records be created from this point forward

questions.explanation: Undocumented modifications are common. The inspector documents what is found, codes against actual condition, and recommends formal records from this point onward. The EICR itself becomes the new baseline document.

questions.prompt: An EICR identifies an installation where the consumer unit has Type AC RCBOs but the loads include LED drivers and electronic dimmers. Typical code:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Electronic loads can produce DC residual current that Type AC RCDs cannot reliably trip on. The current edition requires Type A as a minimum where DC fault current is possible — typically C2. C3 if there is an established case for low DC content (rare in modern lighting).

questions.prompt: An IR test on a 400 V three-phase circuit. The minimum acceptable IR is:

options.B: 1 MΩ

questions.explanation: Minimum IR for nominal voltages up to 500 V is 1 MΩ (BS 7671 Table 64.1). The test voltage at 400 V nominal is 500 V DC. The 1 MΩ threshold is the same as for 230 V circuits.

questions.prompt: An EICR Schedule of Test Results entry shows R1+R2 = 0.42 Ω, Zs = 0.46 Ω. The implied Ze is approximately:
questions.explanation: Ze = Zs − (R1+R2) = 0.46 − 0.42 = 0.04 Ω. A very low Ze suggests a TN-C-S supply with a parallel earth path (for example, bonded metallic services). The result is consistent with a typical urban TN-C-S installation.

questions.prompt: Continuity of CPCs is tested using:

options.A: A low-resistance ohmmeter (typically 200 mA test current)
options.B: An IR tester at 500 V DC

questions.explanation: Low-resistance ohmmeter at typical 200 mA test current. The test current overcomes any oxidation on contacts and gives a stable mΩ-range reading. IR, loop and RCD testers are for different tests entirely.

questions.prompt: An EICR finds a domestic installation where the bonding to the gas pipe is in 6 mm² but the supply requires 10 mm² (TN-C-S, supply earth >35 mm² CSA). Typical code:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Undersized main bonding fails to provide the required equipotential at fault. Typically C2 (potentially dangerous). The current edition requires sizing per the supply earth conductor.

questions.prompt: An RCD tested at 5× IΔn must trip within:

options.B: 300 ms regardless of type

questions.explanation: BS EN 61008 general-type RCD: 40 ms at 5× IΔn. Time-delayed S-type has a higher (50-150 ms typical) value. The 5× test ensures the RCD operates fast enough to provide additional protection at high fault current.

questions.prompt: Inspection sampling escalates because:

options.B: Each defect found in the sample increases the likelihood that the unsampled population contains similar defects, requiring confidence to be rebuilt with a larger sample

questions.explanation: Sampling is a confidence exercise. Defects found undermine the assumption that the sample is representative; the only response is a larger sample. Persistent defects justify 100% testing of the affected population.

questions.prompt: An EICR records 'no protective conductor at one socket; circuit otherwise continues to operate'. Typical code:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Missing CPC at a socket means the protective measure is non-functional for any Class I appliance plugged in. Typically C2; can rise to C1 if the socket is in a high-risk area or the metallic accessory could rise to fault potential.

questions.prompt: The inspector cannot complete an RCD trip-time test because the residual-current load is too high (large CPD leakage). The defensible response is:

options.B: Investigate the leakage, code it appropriately if persistent, and either test after remedial work or record it as a limitation/FI with reason

questions.explanation: High residual leakage that prevents testing is itself a finding. The inspector investigates the cause (faulty appliance, accumulated leakage from many electronic loads), codes if persistent, and either retests after remedial action or treats as a limitation/FI.

questions.prompt: An EICR identifies an electrically-heated underfloor heating mat where the IR is below the minimum. Typical code:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Low IR on an underfloor heating mat is potentially dangerous (C2) — the mat is in continuous use with bare feet on the floor above. The cause needs investigation; if exposed conductive parts are at fault potential during use, the code escalates to C1.

questions.prompt: A 6 A Type B MCB has a tabulated maximum Zs of approximately:
questions.explanation: Type B 6 A: Im = 5 × In = 30 A; Zs(table) = 230/30 ≈ 7.67 Ω. The actual figure in BS 7671 Table 41.3 is around 7.67 Ω at full operating temperature. 80% measured equals roughly 6.13 Ω.

questions.prompt: An EICR observes a non-RCD-protected lighting circuit in a domestic installation. Cable is partially concealed in the wall. Typical code:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Cables concealed in walls less than 50 mm deep require RCD protection (Reg 522.6.202). Where the cable is not RCD-protected and is concealed at less than this depth, the code is typically C2. C3 if the cable is in a metal sleeve / earthed enclosure giving compliant routing.

questions.prompt: An EICR has a single FI observation. The overall result:

options.A: Satisfactory because no codes were raised
options.B: Unsatisfactory until the FI is closed out by follow-up investigation

questions.explanation: FI alone makes the report Unsatisfactory. The follow-up investigation may downgrade to a lesser code or remove the concern entirely — but until that closure happens, the report stays Unsatisfactory.

questions.prompt: Periodic inspection of an installation supplying a swimming pool zone — the supplementary equipotential bonding should:

options.A: Be tested for continuity (typically R ≤ 0.05 Ω) between exposed-conductive-parts and extraneous-conductive-parts within the zone
options.B: Be disconnected for the duration of the test
options.D: Be tested with a loop tester only

questions.explanation: Supplementary bonding in special locations is tested for continuity. The accepted threshold is roughly R ≤ 0.05 Ω, ensuring all conductive parts in the zone are at substantially the same potential during a fault.

questions.prompt: A 230 V circuit measures L-E IR = 1.0 MΩ exactly. The defensible response is:

options.B: Investigate further — exactly at the minimum is borderline and may indicate developing fault

questions.explanation: Exactly 1 MΩ meets the legal minimum but is borderline. GN3 recommends investigation — values right at the limit often indicate developing insulation issues, accumulated leakage, or measurement uncertainty.

questions.prompt: An RCD's built-in test button:

options.A: Tests the trip mechanism by simulating a residual current
options.B: Tests the supply voltage

questions.explanation: The built-in test button creates a simulated residual current through an internal resistor. If the RCD trips, the trip mechanism is functional. The button does not test the actual sensitivity or trip times — those need a calibrated tester.

questions.prompt: An EICR finds a 13 A FCU feeding a fixed appliance, but the FCU is wired with the L and N reversed at the FCU output. Typical code:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Reversed polarity at a FCU is potentially dangerous (C2) — the fuse and switch are in the neutral conductor, leaving the fixed appliance unprotected and the live conductor unswitched. Fixing requires re-terminating at the FCU.

questions.prompt: A 2 m radial circuit carrying 10 A has 2.5 mm² cable rated 18 mV/A/m. Voltage drop is approximately:
questions.explanation: Vd = (mV/A/m × A × m) / 1000 = (18 × 10 × 2) / 1000 = 0.36 V. Short runs have negligible voltage drop because length is small; the 5% supply-voltage limit at the load is comfortably met.

questions.prompt: An IR test on a 400 V circuit should be carried out at:

options.B: 500 V DC

questions.explanation: BS 7671 Table 64.1: nominal voltage up to 500 V → IR test voltage 500 V DC, minimum 1 MΩ. SELV/PELV uses 250 V DC and 0.5 MΩ; HV uses 1000 V DC.

questions.prompt: A 25 m run of 1.5 mm² T+E cable carrying 6 A has approximate voltage drop using 29 mV/A/m:
questions.explanation: Vd = (29 × 6 × 25) / 1000 = 4.35 V. Within the 5% limit at 230 V (~11.5 V) but worth checking that combined runs and starting currents are also within limits.

questions.prompt: An EICR finds an installation where the installer has used a screw connection on a stranded conductor without a bootlace ferrule. Typical code:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Stranded conductor in a screw terminal without a ferrule is C3 (improvement recommended) — workmanship issue. Where there is evidence of arcing or loose connection, the code escalates to C2.

questions.prompt: An EICR records 'all RCDs trip well within their permitted times'. The defensible test method for 30 mA RCDs at 5× IΔn:

options.A: Test current 150 mA, max 40 ms (general type)
options.B: Test current 1.5 A, max 40 ms

questions.explanation: 30 mA × 5 = 150 mA test current, max 40 ms for general type per BS EN 61008. The 1× test is at 30 mA / 300 ms; the 5× test ensures rapid disconnection at higher fault current.

questions.prompt: An EICR identifies a corroded earth electrode on a TT installation. Typical code:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Corroded electrode on TT is potentially dangerous — Ra rises and fault disconnection becomes unreliable. Typically C2; if Ra is so high that disconnection cannot occur, the code rises to C1.

questions.prompt: Ra (electrode resistance) on a TT installation should be:

options.A: ≤ 1500 Ω if the RCD is 30 mA, calculated from 50 V / IΔn (typical max in domestic)
options.B: Always 1 Ω or less

questions.explanation: Ra ≤ 50 / IΔn, so for 30 mA RCD: Ra ≤ 50 / 0.030 = 1667 Ω theoretical. Industry guidance often uses ≤ 200 Ω for stability — the lower the better. The 50 V threshold is the touch voltage for normal-condition locations.

questions.prompt: An EICR identifies a distribution board where the labelling on the breakers is mismatched with the actual circuits. Typical code:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Mismatched labelling alone is C3 (improvement recommended) — the installation works, but isolating the right circuit during maintenance is harder than it should be. Improvement: relabel against verified circuit identification.

questions.prompt: An EICR observation that 'a circuit's neutral and CPC are linked at one accessory in error' is typically coded:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: N/CPC linked at an accessory is potentially dangerous (C2) — RCDs may nuisance-trip and fault current is shared between N and CPC. C1 follows where the linking creates an immediate danger or where exposed-conductive-parts are at fault potential.

questions.prompt: Periodic inspection of a privately rented dwelling uncovers a recent DIY alteration with no certificate. The inspector should:

options.A: Document the alteration, code as found (C2/C3/FI depending on actual condition), and recommend a competent person certifies the work
options.B: Refuse the inspection

questions.explanation: DIY alterations are common and need investigating. The inspector codes against actual condition; if the work is non-compliant the code can be C2 or higher. Recommendation: have it certified by a competent person via Building Control or a Part P scheme.

questions.prompt: An EICR finds an installation where the L and N have been swapped at the consumer unit. Typical code:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Reversed L/N at the consumer unit is C1 — every protective device and switch in the installation is now in the neutral conductor; the line is unprotected throughout. Immediate action: make safe and notify the duty holder same-day in writing.

questions.prompt: An EICR observation that 'switches are wired in the neutral conductor on certain lighting circuits' is typically coded:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Switches in the neutral are potentially dangerous (C2) — the line conductor remains live to the lampholder when the switch is off, exposing anyone changing a bulb. Typical fix: rewire the switch in the line conductor.

questions.prompt: An EICR finds a TN-C-S installation where the supply earth has been disconnected at the consumer unit. The installation continues to function. Typical code:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Disconnected supply earth on TN-C-S means the protective measure is not functional — fault disconnection cannot be assured. C1 (immediate danger). Make safe and notify same-day in writing.

questions.prompt: On an IR test, L-E reads 50 MΩ but L-N reads 0.3 MΩ. The defensible interpretation is:

options.A: There is a fault between the line and neutral — investigate further
options.B: Pass — both above the minimum

questions.explanation: L-N below 1 MΩ is a fault. The high L-E reading rules out an earth fault at the same point but the low L-N is significant — typically a load left connected, an installed component (capacitor, MOV), or a wiring fault. Investigate before recording.

questions.prompt: An EICR identifies a circuit feeding a freezer in a privately rented dwelling on the same RCD as other circuits. The freezer trips once a week causing food loss. Typical observation:

options.A: Code as a C3 only (improvement recommended — segregate freezer onto a dedicated RCD/RCBO)
options.B: Code as a C1 (immediate danger)

questions.explanation: Nuisance-tripping affecting a freezer is improvement recommended (C3). Segregating the freezer onto a dedicated RCBO removes the nuisance and minimises losses. It is not in itself dangerous; the RCD is functioning correctly.

questions.prompt: An EICR finds a circuit where the protective conductor has been broken inside a junction box. Typical code:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Broken CPC means the protective measure is non-functional for that circuit. Typically C1 — immediate danger if the circuit feeds Class I equipment. Make safe (typically isolate) and notify same-day.

questions.prompt: An EICR identifies a circuit with extra-low voltage equipment (12 V LEDs) where the isolating transformer is rated 230/12 V but is unfused on the secondary. Typical code:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Unfused secondary on a SELV / PELV transformer is typically C3 (improvement recommended) — modern transformers integrate secondary protection, but the absence does not in itself create danger because the secondary is at extra-low voltage.

questions.prompt: An EICR records 'an RCD trips at exactly its rated residual current'. Per BS EN 61008 the test current at 1× IΔn:

options.A: May or may not trip the RCD — the standard does not require tripping at 1× IΔn, only that it must trip within 300 ms if it does
options.B: Must trip within 40 ms

questions.explanation: BS EN 61008 says an RCD must trip between 0.5× and 1× IΔn — so at exactly 1× IΔn the RCD may or may not trip. If it does, the trip time must be within 300 ms (general type). The 5× test is the more reliable functional check.

questions.prompt: An EICR finds a TN-S installation with the sheath of the incoming cable used as the means of earthing. The sheath shows signs of corrosion. Typical code:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Corroded TN-S earth sheath is potentially dangerous (C2) — the earth path may have high impedance and fault disconnection becomes unreliable. C1 if Zs measurements confirm the impedance is high enough that disconnection cannot occur.

questions.prompt: The voltage drop limit for a final circuit on a domestic installation, per BS 7671 Appendix 4:
questions.explanation: Appendix 4: lighting circuits 3%, other circuits 5% on a public LV supply (domestic typical). The lighting limit is tighter because flicker and dimming are noticeable to the user; sockets etc. tolerate larger drop.

questions.prompt: An EICR identifies an installation where IR tests are deferred because of connected sensitive electronic loads (e.g. a controller that cannot be IR-tested). The defensible response is:

options.A: Disconnect the sensitive load if possible, IR-test the circuit, reconnect; if disconnection is impossible, record as a limitation with reason and consider FI for the un-tested portion
options.B: Apply IR test anyway

questions.explanation: Sensitive electronics cannot be IR-tested at 500 V DC. Standard practice: disconnect, IR test, reconnect. Where disconnection is not possible, record as a limitation; if there is a specific concern that cannot be addressed, raise FI.

questions.prompt: An EICR finds an installation where the consumer unit is correctly bonded but the gas pipe bonding is loose at the gas-pipe terminal. Typical code:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Loose main bonding at the gas pipe is potentially dangerous (C2) — equipotential at fault is compromised. The fix is straightforward (tighten and confirm continuity), but the symptom is significant and warrants C2 coding.

questions.prompt: An EICR identifies a circuit feeding a fish tank pump in a domestic installation, with no RCD. Typical code:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Fish tank circuits without RCD are potentially dangerous (C2). Water + electricity + accessible exposed parts is the classic case for additional protection. Type A or AC RCD at 30 mA is the typical fix.
