options.D: Satisfactory if the cables are insulated

questions.explanation: Metal containment used to support insulated cables is treated as exposed-conductive-part if it could become live under fault. It must be earthed via a dedicated CPC or bonded; absence is potentially dangerous, typically C2.

questions.prompt: On an EICR, a socket-outlet's earth pin is found to be loose and not making reliable contact with the plug's earth. The most appropriate code is:

options.B: C2 (typical) — fault protection on the connected appliance could be defeated
options.C: C1 (where the appliance is Class I and routinely used by ordinary persons)
options.D: Either B or C depending on use and accessibility

questions.explanation: BPG4 again: poor earth contact at a socket can be C2 where it's a passive defect, or C1 if the connected appliance is Class I and frequently used. The inspector documents the use case and codes accordingly.

questions.prompt: An EICR finds a TT-system installation with no RCD between the consumer unit and the means of earthing. The most appropriate code is:

options.B: C2
options.C: C1 — TT systems require RCD as the only practical means of fault protection
options.D: Satisfactory if the earth electrode resistance is low

questions.explanation: TT systems rely on RCD for fault protection (because earth electrode loop impedance is generally too high for an MCB to meet disconnection times). Absence of RCD on a TT is C1 per BPG4 — the protective measure is essentially absent.

questions.prompt: An EICR finds a junction box used in a maintained location, accessible for inspection but containing a connection that has been wrapped in insulating tape rather than terminated in a proper terminal. The most appropriate code is:

options.B: C2 — improperly terminated joint, risk of failure / overheating
options.C: C1 if visibly hot or showing signs of arcing
options.D: Either B or C depending on the joint's current condition

questions.explanation: Tape-wrapped joints are unreliable and can deteriorate to a high-resistance fault. Cool, intact, securely insulated joints are typically C2; hot or visibly arcing joints lift to C1 with on-site make-safe.

questions.prompt: An EICR observation reads 'Bath and basin in a dwelling installed but no main protective bonding to plumbing — extraneous-conductive-part status not yet confirmed'. The most appropriate code is:

options.B: FI — extraneous-conductive-part status must be confirmed before a code can be applied

questions.explanation: Where the extraneous-conductive-part status is genuinely unknown (modern plastic plumbing may not require bonding), an FI is appropriate. Once confirmed extraneous, missing bonding is C2; if confirmed not extraneous, no observation.

questions.prompt: An EICR finds an exposed metal back box at a switch position with a damaged faceplate. Live terminal accessible. The most appropriate code is:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Accessible live terminal is C1 — basic protection failed. The inspector should isolate the circuit and label it before leaving site, regardless of how rarely the switch is used.

questions.prompt: An EICR observation reads 'BS 3036 rewireable fuse remaining on a 5 A lighting circuit in original 1960s installation, otherwise sound'. The most appropriate code is:

options.B: C2
options.C: C3 — improvement recommended (older protective device technology, current edition expects HBC fuses or MCBs)
options.D: Satisfactory unless ADS times cannot be met

questions.explanation: BPG4: a BS 3036 fuse that still meets BS 7671 disconnection times for the circuit is generally Satisfactory or C3 (improvement recommended). The inspector confirms ADS performance via Zs measurement; if ADS is impaired, the call rises to C2.

questions.prompt: An EICR finds a domestic kitchen with no RCD additional protection on the socket-outlets. The most appropriate code is:

options.A: C3 if the installation is plainly a long-standing legacy install
options.B: C2 (typical) — current BS 7671 requires additional protection on socket-outlets accessible to ordinary persons up to 32 A
options.D: Either A or B depending on the inspector's judgement of the installation's age and recent works

questions.explanation: BPG4 typically calls C2 in a current dwelling without RCD additional protection on accessible sockets; some inspectors apply C3 to genuinely untouched older installations. The current consensus favours C2 for any domestic install in active use.

questions.prompt: An EICR finds an undersized CPC on a circuit (e.g. 1.0 mm² CPC on a 4.0 mm² 32 A radial), with no parallel earth path and Zs at the limit. The most appropriate code is:

options.B: C2 (typical) — adiabatic check fails / CPC inadequate for fault current

questions.explanation: An undersized CPC may not survive the fault current within the protective device's clearance time. The protective measure is impaired. C2: replace with adequately sized CPC or upgrade the protective device.

questions.prompt: On an EICR, an item that has previously been coded C2 and remediated should be:

options.A: Coded C2 again on the new EICR
options.B: Coded C3 to acknowledge previous concern
options.C: Recorded as remediated, with the new EICR coding the current observed condition (typically Satisfactory if the remedy was effective)

questions.explanation: Each EICR captures the current condition. A previously fixed C2 that is now compliant is Satisfactory on the new report. The previous observation lives in the previous report; the new report doesn't carry it forward unless the issue has recurred.

questions.prompt: An EICR finds a domestic CU with mixed device types — one MCB, one RCBO and a wirewound BS 1361 fuse, all from different manufacturers. The most appropriate observation is:

options.A: C2 — manufacturer mixing impairs the assembly
options.B: C3 (typical) — improvement recommended (mixing devices outside the CU's listed range is typically a manufacturer-conformance / BPG4 issue rather than an immediate danger)

questions.explanation: Mixing devices that are not listed as compatible with the CU is a manufacturer-conformance concern. Where the protective measures still operate correctly the typical call is C3 with a recommendation for matched devices.

questions.prompt: An EICR finds visible arcing inside a distribution board cover on a factory site. The most appropriate code is:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Visible arcing is an immediate danger. The inspector must isolate the affected board and label it before leaving site, then code C1 with a clear description for the duty holder.

questions.prompt: An EICR finds an SPD (surge protection device) with the status indicator showing 'replace'. The most appropriate code is:

options.B: C2 — surge protective measure not effective
options.C: C3 (typical) — improvement recommended (the SPD is past end-of-life and should be replaced; current edition recommends SPD where appropriate)

questions.explanation: An SPD past end-of-life still allows the rest of the installation to operate, but no longer provides surge protection. Typical BPG4 call is C3 — improvement recommended; replace the SPD module.

questions.prompt: An EICR finds a circuit's polarity reversed at the consumer unit (line and neutral swapped) so single-pole MCBs are now in the neutral conductor. The most appropriate code is:

options.B: C2
options.C: C1 — protective device is in the wrong conductor; isolation switching does not break the line

questions.explanation: Reversed polarity at the CU defeats single-pole isolation entirely — the line stays connected when the MCB is open. This is dangerous and the inspector should isolate at the main switch, label, and code C1.

questions.prompt: An EICR observation reads 'Tested with all loads connected; cannot determine whether low IR is from electronic loads or installation fault'. The most appropriate code is:

options.B: FI — further investigation required by isolating loads and re-testing

questions.explanation: FI is the right code when the inspector cannot determine the cause during the inspection. A follow-up visit with electronic loads isolated will produce a clean reading; until then the report is Unsatisfactory.

questions.prompt: An EICR finds a Class I metal kitchen appliance plugged into a socket with no earth pin contact (the socket's earth contact is broken). The most appropriate code is:

options.B: C2 — fault protection on the appliance is defeated
options.C: C1 (typical) — Class I appliance with no earth, danger present in domestic kitchen use by ordinary persons

questions.explanation: A Class I appliance relies on the CPC to clear faults to the metal body. With no earth at the socket, a fault could leave the appliance body live indefinitely. C1: isolate, label, replace the socket.

questions.prompt: An EICR finds a 50-year-old TN-S installation's main earthing conductor as a 4 mm² bare copper strap, undersized for current BS 7671 sizing. The most appropriate code is:

options.B: C2 — earthing conductor may be inadequate for current fault levels
options.C: C1 if the installation has obviously been modified to higher fault current capacity
options.D: FI to verify the historical sizing

questions.explanation: Under-sized main earthing conductor is potentially dangerous — fault current may exceed conductor capacity and damage / open the earth path. C2: upgrade to BS 7671 Table 54.7 minimum.

questions.prompt: An EICR finds an isolator on the immersion heater circuit fitted as a single-pole switch. The most appropriate code is:

options.B: C2 (likely) — isolation switching incomplete (BS 7671 requires double-pole isolation for water heaters)

questions.explanation: Water heaters are typically required to be capable of all-pole isolation (BS 7671 Reg 537 / older 514). A single-pole isolator can leave the neutral connected during maintenance, with shock risk. C2: replace with a DP isolator.

questions.prompt: An EICR finds a 30 mA RCD providing additional protection on a circuit feeding several outdoor sockets. The RCD trips at 1×IΔn within 250 ms and at 5×IΔn within 32 ms. The most appropriate record is:

options.B: C3
options.C: Satisfactory — both readings within BS 7671 limits

questions.explanation: ≤300 ms at 1×IΔn and ≤40 ms at 5×IΔn. The RCD is operating correctly; schedule entry is Satisfactory.

questions.prompt: An EICR finds an exposed conductor at the back of a luminaire's flex outlet that protrudes through the protective sleeve. The most appropriate code is:

options.B: C2 — basic protection compromised
options.C: C1 (typical) — exposed live conductor at an accessible location

questions.explanation: Exposed live conductor at an accessible point is C1 regardless of where the access is. The inspector should isolate the circuit and label it before leaving site.

questions.prompt: An EICR finds a metal-clad domestic CU with a small surface scratch on the door but otherwise sound. The most appropriate observation is:

options.B: C3
options.C: Satisfactory — cosmetic only, no protective measure compromised

questions.explanation: Cosmetic scratches that don't compromise the IP rating, basic protection or fire containment are not coded. The inspector may note the scratch in the schedule for completeness but the result is Satisfactory.

questions.prompt: An EICR finds that a circuit's RCD has been jumpered out (the RCD's output connections shorted together). The most appropriate code is:

options.B: C2
options.C: C1 — protective device deliberately defeated, danger present

questions.explanation: Deliberate defeat of a protective device is a serious C1: the protection has been removed entirely. The inspector must isolate, label and notify the duty holder same day.

questions.prompt: An EICR observation reads 'Cable concealed in stud wall, route unknown, no detection possible during inspection'. The most appropriate code is:

options.B: C3
options.C: FI — further investigation required to establish route compliance

questions.explanation: Where the inspector cannot determine cable routing and the route's compliance with safe-zone / depth requirements is uncertain, FI is appropriate. The investigation may use cable detectors or open-up access to confirm.

questions.prompt: An EICR finds an obvious DIY-quality joint at an exposed loft-level cable run, made with twisted-and-taped conductors. The most appropriate code is:

options.B: C2 (typical) — joint not made in a suitable enclosure / using suitable terminals
options.C: C1 if the joint is currently exposed and accessible
options.D: Either B or C depending on the joint's accessibility and condition

questions.explanation: BPG4: a non-compliant joint that is currently insulated and not accessible may be C2 (potentially dangerous, foreseeable progression). A joint with exposed live parts at the time of inspection is C1 with on-site make-safe.

questions.prompt: An EICR finds a circuit feeding a fixed mobility-aid charging point in a sheltered-housing dwelling, with no RCD protection. The most appropriate code is:

options.B: C2 — additional protection required for circuits used by ordinary persons / vulnerable occupants

questions.explanation: Fixed equipment in sheltered housing accessed by ordinary persons (often vulnerable) requires the protective measures expected of the current edition, including 30 mA RCD additional protection. Absence is potentially dangerous: C2.

questions.prompt: An EICR observation reads 'Earthing conductor terminated at MET via a cable lug; lug nut hand-tight only, found loose during inspection'. The most appropriate code is:

options.B: C2 — fault protection earth path could be lost under fault or vibration
options.C: C1 if the conductor is so loose that fault protection is currently absent
options.D: Either B or C depending on continuity testing of the joint

questions.explanation: BPG4: a loose earthing termination with continuity intact is typically C2 (re-tighten); a termination so loose that earthing is effectively lost (no continuity, exposed conductor) is C1 with on-site remediation.

questions.prompt: An EICR finds a recently installed PV array DC isolator without correct DC-rated labelling. The most appropriate code is:

options.B: C2 (likely) — incorrect labelling and identification could cause unsafe operation during emergency isolation

questions.explanation: PV systems require correct DC isolation labelling so emergency responders can disconnect safely. Missing or incorrect labelling on a DC isolator is potentially dangerous: C2 — relabel and verify polarity / orientation.

questions.prompt: An EICR finds a cooker control unit with a switched 13 A socket, the socket switch left in the on position with no plug inserted, and the inner shutters non-functional. The most appropriate code is:

options.B: C2 — basic protection compromised at an accessible socket
options.C: C1 (where exposed live terminals are accessible due to non-functional shutters)
options.D: Either B or C depending on whether live terminals are currently accessible

questions.explanation: Non-functional shutters are a basic-protection issue. If a finger or test pin can reach the live terminal, C1; if not currently accessible but shutters are unreliable, C2 with prompt remedy.

questions.prompt: An EICR observation reads 'TN-C-S supply with PME conditions, but no warning notice at consumer unit'. The most appropriate code is:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Missing safety / warning notices are typically C3 — the labelling is required for future safe maintenance, but its absence does not present an immediate danger. Add a PME / TN-C-S notice at the position of the main earthing terminal.

questions.prompt: An EICR finds a recently extended kitchen with a new dishwasher circuit without supplementary RCD protection on the new dishwasher socket. The most appropriate code is:

options.B: C2 — current BS 7671 requires RCD additional protection on socket-outlets used by ordinary persons
options.D: Satisfactory because the dishwasher is fixed equipment

questions.explanation: A socket-outlet (even one feeding a fixed appliance) used by ordinary persons up to 32 A requires 30 mA RCD additional protection per current BS 7671. Absence is C2 — Unsatisfactory and remedy promptly.

questions.prompt: A 30 mA RCBO on a socket circuit gives 1 x IDeltan results of 24 ms and 286 ms, 5 x IDeltan results of 38 ms and 41 ms, and the test button operates. Under current BS 7671-style RCD testing, what is the best interpretation?

options.A: Fail, because every 5 x test must be under 40 ms
options.B: Fail, because one 1 x test exceeded 40 ms
options.C: FI in all cases because the two 1 x results differ
options.D: Acceptable for a general non-delay 30 mA RCBO because the 1 x IDeltan results are below 300 ms; 5 x testing is not the current core pass criterion

questions.explanation: Current-style BS 7671 verification focuses on operation at rated residual current, with a general non-delay RCD operating within 300 ms. Older training rules often used a 5 x 40 ms criterion for additional protection; under that older approach, the 41 ms value would be retested and examined, but it is not the current core pass/fail test in the same way.

questions.prompt: A TT installation has RA = 166 ohm, a 100 mA time-delayed main RCD and 30 mA final-circuit RCDs. Using 50 V as the touch-voltage limit, what is the best assessment of RA?

options.A: It fails because RA must always be below 1 ohm
options.B: It fails for the 30 mA RCD but passes for the 100 mA RCD
options.C: It satisfies RA x IDeltan <= 50 V for both 100 mA and 30 mA devices, but the value is still high enough to merit caution about stability
options.D: It is irrelevant because RCDs do not operate on TT systems

questions.explanation: For 100 mA: 166 ohm x 0.1 A = 16.6 V. For 30 mA: 166 ohm x 0.03 A = 4.98 V. Both are below 50 V. However, high electrode resistance may vary seasonally and can become unreliable, so it should not be treated casually.

questions.prompt: A lighting circuit has R1+R2 = 2.86 ohm. On a TN-C-S installation, measured live Zs at the furthest point is 0.52 ohm. Ze at the origin is 0.21 ohm. What is the best interpretation?

options.A: The measured Zs is suspiciously low and likely influenced by parallel paths; Ze + R1+R2 gives about 3.07 ohm and should be used to assess the actual CPC path
options.B: The measured Zs proves the CPC is excellent, so R1+R2 can be ignored
options.C: The circuit is automatically C1 because all lighting circuits over 2 ohm are immediately dangerous
options.D: N/A because Zs is not relevant to lighting circuits

questions.explanation: A measured live Zs far lower than Ze + R1+R2 suggests parallel paths. Parallel paths must not be relied upon as the circuit CPC. Calculate or assess the true fault loop using the circuit protective conductor path and investigate if ADS cannot be met.

questions.prompt: A final circuit protected by a BS EN 60898 Type B 32 A MCB has measured Zs = 1.21 ohm at ambient temperature and no RCD for fault protection. Without relying on a memorised table value, what is the correct method?

options.A: Accept it if the circuit energises normally
options.B: Identify required disconnection time, determine Ia from the device characteristic or tables, apply Zs <= Uo/Ia, and compare using appropriate temperature/correction adjustments
options.C: Reject it automatically because any Zs over 1 ohm is unsafe
options.D: Use insulation resistance instead of Zs

questions.explanation: Zs acceptability depends on the protective device, required disconnection time and operating current. For a Type B MCB, instantaneous operation is conventionally around 5 x In, but the proper route is device data or tables plus correction for conductor temperature and measurement conditions.

questions.prompt: A privately rented dwelling EICR is Unsatisfactory. The maximum time to remedy is:

options.B: 28 days from the inspection (or sooner if the report specifies)

questions.explanation: PRS Regs 2020: 28 days from the inspection date to remedy or to carry out further investigation, plus written confirmation supplied to the tenant within 28 days of the work, and to the local authority within 7 days of any written request.

questions.prompt: A C2 observation is added to an EICR on a domestic dwelling under PRS Regs 2020. The next-tenancy clock is:

options.B: Independent — the landlord must remediate the C2 within 28 days of the inspection regardless of the next-tenancy date

questions.explanation: The 28-day remedy clock runs from the inspection regardless of tenancy events. A new tenancy doesn't pause the clock; the landlord must hit both deadlines independently.

questions.prompt: A non-domestic duty holder asks the inspector for the make-safe to be held off so business can continue. The inspector should:

options.B: Refuse — make-safe of a known C1 is non-negotiable; offer to coordinate timing of permanent remediation but not the immediate isolation
options.C: Withdraw from the site without making safe

questions.explanation: C1 isolation cannot be deferred for business convenience. The inspector explains the legal position, isolates and labels, records the conversation. Permanent fix can be planned around operational needs once the immediate danger is removed.

questions.prompt: Where remedial work follows an Unsatisfactory EICR, the written confirmation must come from:

options.A: Anyone who picks up the work
options.B: A qualified person — typically a registered competent electrician
options.C: The inspector who issued the EICR

questions.explanation: PRS Regs 2020 require the written confirmation to be provided by a 'qualified person' competent in electrical inspection. This may be the original inspector or another suitably qualified electrician — the key is competence, not identity.

questions.prompt: Under HSWA 1974 / EAWR 1989, the duty holder for a workplace electrical installation is normally:

options.B: The employer or person in control of the workplace, including their senior management chain

questions.explanation: EAWR 1989 places duties on the employer / responsible person in control of the workplace. Senior managers can be personally liable under HSWA / corporate manslaughter legislation if a failure to act on safety reports leads to harm.

questions.prompt: An inspector finds a C2 on a critical circuit and the duty holder cannot fix it before the next inspection. The inspector should:

options.B: Code it C2, document the duty holder's plan and prompt remediation; the EICR remains Unsatisfactory until the C2 is resolved

questions.explanation: Codes reflect observed condition, not the duty holder's plan. The C2 stays, the report is Unsatisfactory, and the remedy / written confirmation flow follows. Re-coding to keep a client happy is professional misconduct.

questions.prompt: Following an Unsatisfactory EICR with a C1 that the inspector has made safe, the duty holder should:

options.B: Arrange permanent remediation, retain the make-safe label and isolation until then, and obtain written confirmation when the work is completed
options.D: Issue an MEIWC for the make-safe

questions.explanation: The make-safe is a temporary measure. The duty holder must commission permanent remediation by a qualified person, then collect written confirmation. The labelled isolation stays in place until the qualified person verifies the fix.

questions.prompt: Local authorities under PRS Regs 2020 can request a copy of the EICR and require it to be supplied within:

options.B: 7 days of a written request

questions.explanation: PRS Regs 2020: local authority written request → 7 days for the landlord to supply the EICR. Failure can trigger enforcement and financial penalty.

questions.prompt: A landlord refuses to act on an Unsatisfactory EICR. The local authority enforcement options include:

options.A: Formal remedial notice and a financial penalty (up to £30,000 per breach)
options.B: Verbal request only

questions.explanation: PRS Regs 2020 give local authorities significant enforcement powers — formal notices to remedy and financial penalties up to £30,000 per breach. Repeat or aggravated breaches can attract additional penalties.

questions.prompt: A non-domestic duty holder under HSWA 1974 fails to act on a known C1 and an injury results. The likely consequences include:

options.A: No action because EICRs are advisory
options.B: HSE investigation, possible prosecution under HSWA / EAWR, civil claims and reputational harm

questions.explanation: HSWA 1974 / EAWR 1989 create criminal and civil liability where a duty holder fails to act on identified risks. Senior managers can face personal prosecution; the organisation can face unlimited fines and reputational harm.

questions.prompt: A C3 observation alone makes the EICR overall:

options.B: Satisfactory with improvements recommended

questions.explanation: C3 alone keeps the report Satisfactory. The duty holder is not legally compelled to act in a regulated timeframe (per PRS Regs / EAWR), but should plan and budget the improvements.

questions.prompt: An EICR is Unsatisfactory and the duty holder asks the inspector for a quick top-up retest after remedial works. The inspector should:

options.B: Carry out a re-inspection of the remedied items and either issue a written confirmation per PRS Regs or update / re-issue the report as appropriate
options.C: Sign a clean report without inspection

questions.explanation: A re-inspection focused on the remedied items, with appropriate testing, can be issued as a written confirmation under PRS Regs or as an updated EICR. The inspector inspects what they sign for.

questions.prompt: A C1 observation always makes the EICR overall:

options.A: Satisfactory because it was made safe
options.B: Unsatisfactory — the original observed condition is what the report records

questions.explanation: Make-safe is a remedy, not a coding override. The EICR records the condition observed; once a C1 has been observed, the report is Unsatisfactory and the duty holder's regulatory obligations flow from that result.

questions.prompt: On a non-domestic premises an EICR with two C2 items is issued. The duty holder's first risk-based step should be:

options.B: Identify which C2 has the higher residual risk and address it first while planning the second; document the prioritisation rationale

questions.explanation: Risk-based prioritisation is the standard EAWR 1989 approach. The duty holder ranks observations by likelihood and severity, addresses the worst first, and keeps a documented trail of decisions and actions taken.

questions.prompt: A landlord receives an EICR Satisfactory result with three C3s. They are required to:

options.A: Remediate within 28 days under PRS Regs 2020
options.B: Plan and execute the C3 improvements over time; PRS Regs do not impose a strict timeframe for C3-only outcomes

questions.explanation: C3-only EICRs are Satisfactory. PRS Regs 2020 don't impose the 28-day clock for C3 improvements; the landlord plans them as good practice and budgets accordingly.

questions.prompt: An inspector finds a C1 on a school's plant room circuit and isolates it. The school's premises manager wants the inspector to leave the keys to the isolation. The correct action is:

options.B: Retain a record of who has the isolation key, ensure the circuit cannot be re-energised by the duty holder until permanent remediation is verified, and document the conversation

questions.explanation: Lock-out / tag-out arrangements protect both the inspector and the duty holder. The inspector ensures the isolation is robust and the re-energisation path requires verified permanent remediation, not informal premises-manager discretion.

questions.prompt: Under PRS Regs 2020, the maximum financial penalty per breach is:
questions.explanation: PRS Regs 2020 — financial penalties up to £30,000 per breach, with multiple breaches potentially compounded. Local authorities have discretion based on severity, history and cooperation.

questions.prompt: An inspector who suspects fraudulent prior certification (e.g. dates altered, signatures forged) on a previous EICR should:

options.B: Document the concern, decline to rely on the suspect document, and report the concern through their professional body / scheme provider where appropriate

questions.explanation: Fraud concerns must be documented and escalated. The inspector cannot rely on fabricated evidence; their professional body has reporting routes. The local authority may need to be informed if it affects PRS compliance.

questions.prompt: On a TT-supplied dwelling, the inspector finds an inoperative RCD. Given TT systems rely on RCDs for fault protection, the appropriate code and on-site action is:

options.B: C1 typically — fault protection is essentially absent; isolate the circuit and notify the duty holder same day

questions.explanation: TT systems depend on RCDs because earth electrode loop impedance is too high for an MCB to clear faults in time. An inoperative RCD on a TT system means no functional fault protection — typically C1 with on-site make-safe and same-day notification.

questions.prompt: An inspector finds an Unsatisfactory result on a school. The duty holder under HSWA 1974 must act in a timeframe that is:

options.A: Always 28 days as for PRS dwellings
options.B: Reasonable and risk-based per HSWA / EAWR — the duty holder must act 'so far as is reasonably practicable' and document the rationale

questions.explanation: HSWA 1974 / EAWR 1989 don't have the 28-day clock. The duty holder applies risk-based prioritisation and acts 'so far as is reasonably practicable'. Documentation of decisions and actions is essential to demonstrate compliance.

questions.prompt: An EICR with no C1, C2, C3 or FI observations is overall:

options.B: Satisfactory

questions.explanation: An EICR with zero observations is straightforwardly Satisfactory — the schedules support that result, the inspector signs and dates the report, and the next-inspection interval is set.

questions.prompt: An EICR with one C3 only is overall:

options.B: Satisfactory with improvement recommended

questions.explanation: C3 alone keeps the report Satisfactory. The duty holder is encouraged to plan the improvement but has no specific 28-day-style obligation under PRS Regs.

questions.prompt: An inspector finds a C1 in a busy retail unit. The customer-facing area cannot be closed. The inspector should:

options.A: Skip the make-safe to avoid disruption
options.B: Isolate the affected circuit and label it; agree with the duty holder how to manage customer access until permanent remediation is in place

questions.explanation: Isolating the affected circuit only is targeted make-safe. The duty holder manages the customer-facing impact (e.g. screening off the affected area, signage). The inspector documents the conversation and the actions taken.

questions.prompt: Following an Unsatisfactory EICR on a privately rented dwelling, the landlord must supply written confirmation of remedial work to the tenant:

options.B: Within 28 days of completion

questions.explanation: PRS Regs 2020: tenant within 28 days of completion of remedial works; local authority within 7 days of any written request. Landlords usually keep a single dossier (EICR + remedial confirmation + invoices) to make compliance easy to demonstrate.

questions.prompt: An inspector who is also the duty holder for the same installation should:

options.B: Recognise the conflict of interest and either decline the inspection or arrange independent verification of their findings

questions.explanation: Conflicts of interest undermine the report's credibility. Best practice is to engage an independent inspector; if that's not possible, the inspector / duty holder must declare the conflict and, where appropriate, have the report independently reviewed.

questions.prompt: A landlord supplies the local authority with a copy of the EICR within the required time but ignores the C2 observations beyond 28 days. The local authority can:

options.B: Issue a remedial notice and impose financial penalties up to £30,000 per breach
options.D: Force the landlord to demolish the property

questions.explanation: Compliance is the whole package — supplying the report and acting on Unsatisfactory findings. Failure on the action side is a separate breach with its own enforcement route, regardless of paperwork compliance.

questions.prompt: Under EAWR 1989, the duty to inspect and maintain in non-domestic premises:

options.B: Falls on the duty holder, who must arrange suitable inspection and maintenance regimes 'so far as is reasonably practicable'

questions.explanation: EAWR 1989 places the legal duty on the employer / duty holder to ensure systems are constructed, maintained and used safely. Inspection regimes (EICRs at appropriate intervals) form part of demonstrating compliance.

questions.prompt: An EICR observation that is downgraded by the inspector from C2 to C3 to keep the report Satisfactory is:

options.A: Acceptable if the inspector explains why
options.B: Professional misconduct — codes reflect observed condition, not desired outcome
options.C: Acceptable if the duty holder agrees
options.D: Acceptable if a regulatory body asks for it

questions.explanation: Coding decisions are professional judgements based on BPG4. Downgrading to please the client is misconduct and exposes the inspector to civil and regulatory sanction. The right answer is to code accurately and let the duty holder act.

questions.prompt: An EICR is issued on a non-domestic premises with one FI. The duty holder under EAWR 1989 should:

options.B: Arrange the further investigation without undue delay; the EICR is Unsatisfactory until the FI is resolved

questions.explanation: FI = Unsatisfactory. The duty holder must arrange the investigation, take any further action it indicates, and obtain confirmation that the matter is resolved. Until then, the installation is in an unverified state.

questions.prompt: On a domestic EICR, the inspector advises the tenant of a C1 directly because the landlord cannot be reached. The inspector should:

options.B: Inform the tenant of the immediate safety issue and the make-safe action, document the inability to reach the landlord, and continue trying to notify the duty holder

questions.explanation: The inspector's primary contact is the duty holder, but where the tenant's safety is at risk and the landlord is unreachable, the inspector ensures the tenant understands the immediate safety position and the make-safe action taken. Documentation of attempts to reach the landlord is essential.

questions.prompt: An inspector finds a C2 and the duty holder asks 'Can I just leave it for next time?'. The correct response is:

options.B: No — the EICR is Unsatisfactory, and the duty holder's obligations under PRS Regs / EAWR / HSWA require remediation in a defined or risk-based timeframe
options.D: Yes if the next inspection is soon

questions.explanation: C2 doesn't have a 'next time' option. The Unsatisfactory result triggers the duty holder's regulatory obligation to act — 28 days for PRS dwellings, risk-based for non-domestic premises under HSWA / EAWR.

questions.prompt: A landlord obtains an EICR result they don't agree with and asks the inspector to alter it. The inspector should:

options.B: Decline; the inspector's signature is a professional declaration. If the landlord wants a second opinion they can engage a different inspector

questions.explanation: Each EICR is the inspector's own work. Disagreement is resolved by a fresh inspection by another qualified inspector, not by altering the original report. The original inspector keeps their report intact.

questions.prompt: Under PRS Regs 2020, an Unsatisfactory EICR's 28-day clock starts from:

options.A: The date the landlord receives the report
options.B: The date of the inspection (i.e. when the inspector was on site)
options.D: The end of the financial year

questions.explanation: The clock starts on the date of the inspection, not the date the report is delivered. Landlords should not rely on slow report delivery to extend the clock — the inspection date is what counts.

questions.prompt: An inspector who agrees to issue a Satisfactory EICR after a known C2 has been remediated must:

options.A: Issue the new report without re-inspection
options.B: Re-inspect and re-test the remedied items, confirm the C2 has been resolved, and reissue / update the EICR or written confirmation accordingly
options.D: Charge the duty holder for a new full EICR

questions.explanation: Re-issued / updated reports must be backed by re-inspection of the items that changed. The inspector signs for what they have actually verified — written confirmation of remedial works requires actual verification.

questions.prompt: A C2 on a hospital theatre circuit cannot be remedied without a planned-shutdown window of three months. The duty holder must:

options.A: Ignore the C2 because it's hard to fix
options.B: Document risk-based interim controls (e.g. additional monitoring, restricted use), plan and book the shutdown, and keep the EICR record open with progress notes

questions.explanation: Hospital duty holders must demonstrate risk-based action under HSWA / EAWR. Interim controls reduce residual risk while the planned shutdown is arranged. The EICR remains Unsatisfactory and the trail of evidence supports the duty holder's compliance position.

questions.prompt: An EICR is Unsatisfactory because of a single FI on a privately rented dwelling. The landlord must:

options.A: Treat the FI as a C3
options.B: Arrange the further investigation within 28 days and obtain written confirmation that any defect found has been resolved

questions.explanation: FI is treated like C1/C2 for outcome purposes — the report is Unsatisfactory and the 28-day clock applies. The landlord arranges the investigation, addresses anything found, and produces written confirmation of resolution.

questions.prompt: An inspector finds a C1 in a property they were not contracted to inspect (e.g. an adjacent shop unit during an EICR on the next-door unit). The inspector should:

options.B: Document the observation, ensure immediate make-safe of the danger if accessible, and notify the duty holder of the affected unit and the contracting client

questions.explanation: Knowledge of immediate danger triggers a duty to act regardless of scope. The inspector makes safe within their reach, documents the observation, and notifies the relevant duty holder. Walking away from a known C1 is not an option even outside the inspection scope.

questions.prompt: On a non-domestic premises, the inspector confirms a C2 and the duty holder commits to remediation 'within a couple of weeks' but signs no formal record. The inspector should:

options.B: Record the commitment in the EICR / cover letter so there is a written record of the duty holder's expressed intent and the date

questions.explanation: Verbal commitments are easy to forget in litigation. A written record (in the EICR cover letter, follow-up email or signed cover sheet) protects both parties and supports the duty holder's compliance trail.

questions.prompt: Following an Unsatisfactory EICR on a domestic dwelling, the landlord can demonstrate compliance by:

options.B: Producing the EICR plus written confirmation from a qualified person that the remedial / further investigative work has been done within 28 days

questions.explanation: Compliance documentation = original EICR + qualified person's written confirmation. Invoices are not enough; the confirmation needs to be from someone competent (typically a registered electrician) and must address the specific Unsatisfactory observations.

questions.prompt: An EICR issued on a non-domestic premises whose duty holder also runs other premises in the same chain should be:

options.A: Copied to all premises in the chain
options.B: Treated as relating only to the inspected premises; other premises require their own inspections
options.C: Used as evidence the others are compliant

questions.explanation: Each EICR covers a specific installation. A chain duty holder needs separate inspections for each site to demonstrate compliance with HSWA / EAWR / PRS as applicable. Pattern findings across the chain may inform group-wide remedial planning, however.

questions.prompt: An EICR is Satisfactory with five C3s on an office. The duty holder under HSWA 1974 / EAWR 1989 should:

options.B: Plan the C3 improvements over time as a maintenance / capital programme; document the plan

questions.explanation: C3s are improvement recommendations. Sensible duty holders capture them in a planned maintenance programme so the installation steadily improves between EICRs. HSWA / EAWR don't impose a strict timeframe but expect demonstrable management of identified risks.

questions.prompt: An inspector identifies a C1 at a hospital and the duty holder denies the issue and asks the inspector to leave site without making safe. The inspector should:

options.B: Record the conversation, isolate the affected circuit before leaving (where they have access), notify the duty holder in writing the same day, and consider escalation through the inspector's professional / scheme provider

questions.explanation: Make-safe is not optional. The inspector documents the duty holder's response, makes safe within their access rights, sends written notification, and escalates through scheme providers if necessary. Walking away from a known C1 because a duty holder is unhappy is not professionally defensible.

questions.prompt: On a privately rented dwelling, where the EICR is Satisfactory but recommends the next inspection in 3 years rather than the maximum 5, the landlord should:

options.B: Comply with the inspector's 3-year recommendation; PRS Regs reference the inspector's recommended interval

questions.explanation: The inspector's recommended interval is the upper limit. The landlord follows it; the 5-year regulatory maximum is the floor in absence of a shorter recommendation. Inspectors pull intervals shorter when condition justifies — duty holders honour the recommendation.

questions.prompt: An inspector who deliberately misrecords a C1 as a C3 to keep a customer happy is:

options.B: Committing professional misconduct, exposing themselves to civil and regulatory liability if injury results
options.C: Acting in the duty holder's best interests

questions.explanation: Mis-coding is professional misconduct. If injury follows, the inspector faces personal civil and potential criminal liability. Insurers and scheme providers may also withdraw cover / accreditation on discovery.

questions.prompt: A landlord asks the inspector for a quick re-issue of an Unsatisfactory EICR with the C2 'just removed'. The inspector should:

options.B: Refuse — the C2 reflects the observed condition. Re-issue follows verified remedy, not editing the original report

questions.explanation: Reports are not editable artefacts of a previous inspection. The verified-remedy route is: remediate, re-inspect, written confirmation. Editing the original report retroactively would be falsification.

questions.prompt: Under PRS Regs 2020, a landlord who fails to provide an EICR to a new tenant before they move in:

options.B: Is in breach of the regulations and exposed to local authority enforcement / penalty
options.D: Has no obligation if the tenant doesn't ask

questions.explanation: PRS Regs 2020: new tenants must receive the EICR before move-in. Failure is a discrete breach attracting the same enforcement / penalty regime as failing to remediate Unsatisfactory findings.

questions.prompt: An EICR with one C2 and four C3s on a non-domestic premises means the duty holder must:

options.B: Address the C2 promptly per HSWA / EAWR risk-based principles; the C3s are improvement recommendations to plan over time

questions.explanation: The C2 drives the Unsatisfactory result and demands prompt action. The C3s do not have a regulatory clock but should be planned. Duty holders document their decisions and timelines to demonstrate compliance with EAWR / HSWA.

questions.prompt: An inspector finds a C2 on the same day as a follow-up inspection scheduled for next week. The C2 should be:

options.B: Recorded immediately on this report; the duty holder's clock starts from this inspection date

questions.explanation: Each inspection's findings stand on the date of that inspection. The C2 enters this EICR, the report is Unsatisfactory, and the remedy clock runs from this inspection date. Future inspections are separate snapshots.

questions.prompt: On a domestic EICR, an FI is recorded for an unverified low IR reading. The landlord under PRS Regs 2020 must:

options.B: Arrange further investigation within 28 days, address any defect found, and obtain written confirmation

questions.explanation: FI counts as Unsatisfactory. The 28-day clock applies. The landlord engages a qualified person to do the investigation, addresses any defect, and produces the written confirmation.

questions.prompt: A non-domestic duty holder who relies on an EICR with multiple Operational Limitations (large parts of the installation excluded) is:

options.B: Aware of an evidence gap — the Operational Limitations explicitly say what was not inspected; the duty holder must arrange a separate plan to cover those areas
options.C: Free of regulatory duty for limited areas
options.D: Required to issue a new EICR weekly

questions.explanation: Limitations carve scope out of the inspection. The duty holder retains the legal duty under HSWA / EAWR to maintain safety in the limited areas; they must plan a route to inspect them (out-of-hours, planned shutdown) so the gap is closed.

questions.prompt: An EICR on a privately rented dwelling has been issued with a 'Satisfactory' result and three C3s. The landlord supplies the EICR to the tenant within 28 days. The compliance position is:

options.B: Compliant — Satisfactory result, EICR delivered within timeframe; C3s are improvements to plan but no specific PRS clock

questions.explanation: Satisfactory + EICR delivered in 28 days = compliant. The landlord can plan the C3 improvements at sensible intervals and isn't subject to the 28-day remediation clock that applies to Unsatisfactory results.

questions.prompt: A landlord challenges an inspector's C2 finding. The inspector's response should be:

options.B: Stand behind the professional judgement, explain the BPG4 reasoning and the protective measure concerned, and offer the landlord a second opinion through another qualified inspector

questions.explanation: Codes are professional judgements. The inspector explains their reasoning (which protective measure is impaired, why current edition would expect different) and welcomes a second opinion. Reducing the code under pressure is misconduct.

questions.prompt: An inspector identifies a C1 in an unoccupied retail unit being prepared for fit-out. The duty holder is the landlord, not the incoming tenant. The inspector should:

options.A: Wait for the tenant to move in
options.B: Notify the landlord (current duty holder) immediately, make safe, and ensure the C1 is documented before the new tenant takes occupation

questions.explanation: The current duty holder (landlord) gets notified and the make-safe takes effect now. The incoming tenant inherits a safe installation; the EICR with the documented C1 (and its remediation) becomes part of the property's compliance record.

questions.prompt: An inspector finds a duty holder has hidden previous EICRs that showed C2s. The current EICR records the same C2s persisting. The inspector should:

options.B: Document the persistence of the C2 observations on the current report and note that prior reports have not been acted upon — the duty holder's regulatory exposure is heightened

questions.explanation: The current EICR records what the inspector currently sees. Persistence of unaddressed observations strengthens the case for action; documenting that earlier reports went unactioned (where the inspector has evidence) is a fair professional record. Decisions about local authority engagement sit with the duty holder.

questions.prompt: An EICR's 'Outcome' field is populated based on:

options.B: Whether any C1, C2 or FI is present (Unsatisfactory) versus none of those (Satisfactory)

questions.explanation: Binary outcome logic — drives the duty holder's regulatory action. C3 quantity does not change the outcome. Inspectors should never blur this — it is the cleanest, most useful single field on the report.

questions.prompt: An EICR Satisfactory result on a domestic dwelling with C3s does not relieve the landlord of:

options.B: The general obligation to maintain the installation in safe condition (per the tenancy and consumer protection law); C3s indicate areas where future investment is sensible
options.D: The need to renew the tenancy

questions.explanation: PRS Regs 2020 + general consumer protection / tenancy law expect the dwelling to be safe over time. C3s flag where the installation is below current expectations; sensible landlords plan the investment to keep the dwelling current.

questions.prompt: Under EAWR 1989, an inspector who provides clearly negligent advice that leads to injury can:

options.B: Be personally pursued under HSWA / EAWR, civil law and professional indemnity insurance
options.C: Disclaim liability via a 'best endeavours' clause

questions.explanation: Clear negligence opens personal civil and potentially criminal liability. Standard professional indemnity insurance covers civil claims; criminal prosecution is rare but possible for gross failures. Documentation, BPG4 alignment and care reduce exposure.

questions.prompt: An inspector's commentary on an EICR mentions that 'all observations should be acted on within 12 months'. This statement is:

options.B: Misleading — C1, C2 and FI demand prompt or 28-day action under PRS Regs / risk-based action under EAWR; only C3 is genuinely a 'plan over time' category

questions.explanation: The 12-month blanket statement obscures the urgency of C1/C2/FI. The inspector's commentary should distinguish urgency by code — duty holders need clear direction, not a flat timescale.

questions.prompt: An EICR Satisfactory result with no observations does not relieve the duty holder of:

options.B: Future maintenance, future inspection cycles, and the obligation to act on conditions that develop after the inspection date
options.C: The need to display the report

questions.explanation: An EICR is a snapshot. The duty holder must continue to maintain, inspect at the recommended interval, and act on any conditions that develop. The Satisfactory result is not a 5-year holiday.

questions.prompt: An inspector who refuses to make safe a known C1 because the duty holder hasn't paid the invoice is:

options.B: Acting recklessly — payment terms do not absolve a duty to make safe known immediate danger

questions.explanation: A known C1 must be made safe regardless of commercial dispute. Payment recovery is a separate civil matter; the safety duty is paramount. Walking away from a known C1 over an invoice is reckless and indefensible.

questions.prompt: An EICR is Unsatisfactory and the duty holder has actioned all C2 items but one C1 remains because the part needed is on backorder. The inspector should:

options.B: Confirm interim isolation/make-safe is intact, document the position, and issue an updated record only when the part is fitted and tested

questions.explanation: C1 stays C1 until the danger is permanently removed. Interim controls (isolation, labelling, restricted access) are the bridge; the inspector signs off the closure only after permanent fix and verification.

questions.prompt: A landlord has the EICR but cannot find a 'qualified person' for the remedial work within 28 days. They should:

options.B: Make best endeavours, document attempts, contact alternative qualified persons promptly, and supply the local authority with progress evidence on request — the legal duty remains
options.D: Tell the tenant to wait indefinitely

questions.explanation: PRS Regs 2020 don't have a formal extension mechanism. Local authorities consider best-endeavours evidence on enforcement; the duty holder needs to demonstrate genuine attempts to comply, not silent inaction.

questions.prompt: An EICR's '14C' field — Recommended Date for Next Inspection — is set by:

options.B: The inspector, based on the type of premises, observed condition, environment and BPG4 / GN3 guidance

questions.explanation: The next-inspection date is the inspector's professional call. BPG4 / GN3 give defaults; observed condition, environment and use justify pulling the interval shorter where appropriate.

questions.prompt: Under HSWA 1974, senior managers of a non-domestic duty holder who knowingly ignore C2 findings can be:

options.A: Personally prosecuted under section 37 (corporate offences) if the failure was attributable to them
options.B: Promoted

questions.explanation: HSWA section 37: where a corporate offence is attributable to the consent / connivance / neglect of a director or senior manager, that individual can be personally prosecuted in addition to the corporate body. Ignoring known safety findings risks exactly this.

questions.prompt: An inspector signs off on a written confirmation under PRS Regs 2020 stating that remedial works addressing the original C1/C2/FI items have been completed. They must:

options.B: Have personally re-inspected and re-tested the affected items, verified they comply with BS 7671 / safety expectations, and recorded their findings

questions.explanation: Written confirmation is a professional declaration. The signer must have verified the remedial works personally — re-inspection, re-test, documented evidence. Without that, signing is misconduct.

questions.prompt: An EICR Unsatisfactory with one C2 has been remediated by a different electrician. The original inspector is asked to issue the written confirmation. They should:

options.B: Re-inspect the remedied item, verify compliance, and either sign or refuse based on the verified result

questions.explanation: Written confirmation is what the signer can verify. Re-inspection of the remedied item and confirmation of compliance is the basis for signing. Trust without inspection is professional misconduct.

questions.prompt: An EICR is Unsatisfactory with one FI. Investigation reveals no actual defect (the suspect reading was normal once the cause was identified). The duty holder must:

options.B: Obtain written confirmation that the further investigation found no defect and is documented as such; the original EICR should be supplemented to show the closure

questions.explanation: FI investigations sometimes resolve cleanly. The qualified person produces written confirmation explaining what was investigated and why no defect was found. This closes the regulatory loop without further action being required.

questions.prompt: An EICR's Unsatisfactory result is supplied to a new tenant before move-in. The landlord must also:

options.B: Complete remedial works within 28 days of the inspection (or sooner if the report specifies) and supply written confirmation to the tenant within 28 days of completion
options.D: Wait for the tenant to act

questions.explanation: PRS Regs 2020: supply EICR before move-in, remediate within 28 days of inspection, written confirmation within 28 days of completion. The new tenant gets both the original EICR and the remediation evidence.

questions.prompt: An inspector finds an immediate danger (C1) in a school during the half-term holiday with no school staff on site. The inspector should:

options.A: Leave it for the school's return
options.B: Make safe (isolate the affected circuit), label, secure access, and notify the school's duty holder via emergency contact and in writing the same day

questions.explanation: Make-safe doesn't depend on the duty holder being physically present. Use the emergency contact, document the action, send written notification the same day. The C1 stays in the report regardless of how convenient the timing is for the school.

questions.prompt: An inspector who fails to disclose a known conflict of interest (e.g. the duty holder is a close family member) and issues a Satisfactory EICR is:

options.B: Committing professional misconduct that could invalidate the report and expose them to civil / regulatory liability
options.D: Required to disclose only on request

questions.explanation: Conflicts undermine the report's credibility. Best practice is to declare the conflict and either decline the inspection or have the report independently reviewed. Hidden conflicts are professional misconduct.

questions.prompt: On a privately rented dwelling, the landlord's PRS Regs 2020 obligations apply:

options.A: Only at the start of a tenancy
options.B: Throughout the tenancy — EICR at least every 5 years (or sooner per the inspector's recommendation), action on Unsatisfactory findings, supply to tenants and local authority on request
options.C: Only when an inspection is undertaken

questions.explanation: PRS Regs 2020 apply continuously: maintain the cycle, act on findings, retain evidence, supply on request. The 5-year maximum is one element of an ongoing duty.

questions.prompt: A duty holder asks the inspector for a Satisfactory EICR after a quick visual walk-through (no testing). The inspector should:

options.B: Refuse — an EICR requires inspection and testing per BS 7671 and BPG4; a quick visual is not a valid EICR

questions.explanation: An EICR without testing is not an EICR. Visual-only checks may be a separate informal report, but the BS 7671 model EICR requires testing — Zs, RCD operation, IR, polarity, continuity. The inspector cannot issue an EICR from a walk-through.

questions.prompt: A non-domestic duty holder's documented response to an Unsatisfactory EICR should include:

options.B: A risk-based remedial plan, target dates, evidence of work done, and post-remedial verification — kept on file for HSE / EAWR audit

questions.explanation: Compliance with HSWA / EAWR demands a documented trail. Plan + execution + verification + records is the standard package. Auditors will ask for it; insurers will want it; courts will rely on it.

questions.prompt: An inspector finds a C2 on an extraneous-conductive-part bond. The duty holder asks 'Why is this dangerous when the building has worked fine for 30 years?'. The inspector should:

options.B: Explain that the bond is a fault-condition protective measure — under fault, an unbonded extraneous-conductive-part can become live; 30 years of normal operation is not evidence of fault behaviour

questions.explanation: Most protective measures only matter under fault — they don't show in normal operation. The inspector explains the protective principle, the BPG4 reasoning and stands behind the C2. 'It's been fine until now' is not a coding argument.

questions.prompt: An EICR's 'Persons consulted' field can usefully record:

options.B: Names and roles of duty-holder representatives, contractors and others whose input shaped the inspection (e.g. agreed limitations, operational constraints)

questions.explanation: Recording who was consulted helps trace decisions about scope, limitations and safe-working windows. It also supports the duty holder's compliance evidence — useful in any future dispute about what was agreed.

questions.prompt: An inspector finds clear evidence of fire damage on a circuit (charred sheath, melted accessory). The most appropriate code is:

options.B: C2 if the damage is contained and stable; C1 if there is a continuing fire risk or exposed live parts
options.D: Either B or C depending on the inspector's site assessment

questions.explanation: Fire damage demands judgement. Stable, cooled, no exposed live parts can be C2 with prompt remedial action. Active heat, smoke, exposed live parts is C1 with on-site make-safe and same-day notification.

questions.prompt: On a non-domestic premises with multiple Unsatisfactory items, the duty holder may benefit from:

options.B: Engaging the original inspector or another qualified person to scope a remedial-works package, prioritise by risk, and provide written confirmation as items are completed

questions.explanation: Larger remedial-works packages benefit from professional project management. The original inspector or another qualified person can scope, prioritise, deliver and verify — producing a clean compliance trail at the end.

questions.prompt: An EICR observation that is correctly coded but disputed by the duty holder should be:

options.B: Defended by the inspector with reference to BPG4 / current edition; if the dispute persists, a second-opinion EICR by another qualified inspector is the resolution route

questions.explanation: Disputes are resolved by professional dialogue or a second opinion, not by editing reports. The inspector stands behind their judgement; the duty holder is free to engage another qualified person if they want a different view.

questions.prompt: On a privately rented dwelling, the EICR's recommended next inspection is in 3 years. After 3 years, the landlord must:

options.B: Commission a new EICR within the recommended interval to maintain compliance with PRS Regs 2020

questions.explanation: PRS Regs 2020 require routine EICRs at least every 5 years OR sooner if the inspector recommends. The landlord follows the recommended interval — extending to 5 years against the inspector's advice would breach the regulations.

questions.prompt: Under EAWR 1989, an inspector's professional indemnity insurance:

options.A: Replaces the inspector's duty of care
options.B: Provides cover for civil claims arising from professional negligence; it does not absolve the inspector of professional / regulatory duties

questions.explanation: PI insurance is a financial risk-transfer mechanism. It pays out civil claims (subject to policy terms) but doesn't relieve the inspector of their professional duty of care, BPG4 alignment, and BS 7671 / EAWR / HSWA obligations.

sections.title: Section 4 — Condition Reporting: Consolidated EICR Coding

questions.prompt: At a three-phase distribution board, measured single-phase L-N prospective short-circuit current is 3.8 kA and L-E fault current is 2.9 kA. You cannot safely perform a line-line test. What should be recorded or estimated?

options.A: Only 2.9 kA, because earth faults are always the highest value
options.B: Only Ze, because PFC is not relevant at distribution boards
options.C: The average of 3.8 kA and 2.9 kA
options.D: Record the measured values and estimate maximum three-phase/line-line PFC where necessary, commonly as about 2 x L-N = 7.6 kA unless better data is available

questions.explanation: Three-phase boards may have a higher line-line or three-phase fault current than the line-earth fault current. If direct measurement is unsafe, use design data, DNO/manufacturer data or a justified estimate such as twice the measured single-phase L-N value.

questions.prompt: A Type AC RCD protecting a circuit passes the standard AC residual-current trip test. The circuit supplies equipment likely to produce pulsating DC residual current components. What is the correct distinction?

options.A: A passed trip test proves the RCD type is correct for every load
options.B: The RCD has failed and must be coded C1
options.C: Trip testing confirms operation under the test condition; selection may still be unsuitable for the residual current waveform and should be reported, usually C3 or FI depending on evidence
options.D: RCD type is a design matter and must never be reported on an EICR

questions.explanation: Testing and selection are different. The RCD may operate correctly on the tester yet still be unsuitable for the connected equipment's residual current characteristics. The observation should identify the selection issue, not falsely state that the trip-time test failed.

questions.prompt: An EICR was unsatisfactory due to two C2 observations. A week later, another electrician replaces damaged accessories and sends photos. The landlord asks you to change the original EICR to satisfactory. What should happen?

options.A: The original EICR should remain a record of the condition at the time; remedial work should have appropriate certification or written confirmation, and a new/reissued report only if properly verified and clearly dated
options.B: Backdate a satisfactory EICR because the defects no longer exist
options.D: Accept photos as equivalent to full inspection and testing in every case

questions.explanation: An EICR is a factual report at the inspection date. Remedials require their own certification or confirmation. You may issue further documentation only if you have a proper basis for doing so. Do not erase, backdate or rewrite the original history unless correcting a genuine error.

questions.prompt: An EICR observation says: "Old board, no RCDs, no SPD, poor wiring, needs upgrade - C2." What is the best critique?

options.A: It is ideal because one broad C2 saves time
options.B: It is poor: observations should be specific, evidenced, located and separately coded; "old board" and "needs upgrade" are not defects by themselves
options.C: It should always be C1 instead
options.D: It should be N/A because consumer units are outside the EICR

questions.explanation: A defensible report separates defects: missing RCD additional protection where required, inadequate circuit identification, absence of SPD where required, loose/overheated connections, damaged enclosure, and so on. The observation should describe the safety issue, not simply sell an upgrade.

questions.prompt: An exposed live conductor at an accessible loft junction box. Code:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Exposed accessible live parts = C1 regardless of how rarely the loft is entered. The inspector isolates the circuit, labels it and notifies the duty holder same day.

questions.prompt: A bathroom missing supplementary equipotential bonding where the four conditions of Reg 701.415.2 cannot all be met. Code:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Where the omission conditions are not met, supplementary bonding is required; its absence is potentially dangerous (C2) — install bonding to comply.

questions.prompt: A 30 mA RCD trips at 1×IΔn within 280 ms (limit 300 ms) and 35 ms at 5×IΔn (limit 40 ms). Record:

options.B: C3
options.C: Satisfactory — both readings within BS 7671 limits

questions.explanation: Within limits = Satisfactory. The borderline reading at 1×IΔn might invite a future check or trend, but as recorded it satisfies BS 7671 disconnection time requirements.

questions.prompt: A cosmetic chip on the corner of a faceplate, no live parts visible. Code:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Cosmetic damage with no exposed live parts and no progression risk is C3. The accessory should be replaced when convenient; the EICR remains Satisfactory if this is the only issue.

questions.prompt: A circuit's IR test reads 0.4 MΩ between line and earth. Code (likely):

options.B: C2 — below BS 7671 minimum (1 MΩ for in-service)

questions.explanation: Below-limit IR is potentially dangerous; the inspector should isolate suspect electronic loads and re-test, then code C2 if the reading remains low and the cause is identified, or FI if uncertain.

questions.prompt: Misleading label on the consumer unit's main switch (says 'Lighting'). Code:

options.B: C2 if the misidentification could lead to dangerous incorrect isolation

questions.explanation: Most misidentification labels are C3 because the operator can verify operation. Where misidentification could cause unsafe maintenance switching (e.g. circuit not actually isolated despite the label), the call lifts to C2.

questions.prompt: A loose, oxidised bonding clamp on the gas service, continuity intact. Code:

options.B: C2 — mechanical / electrical reliability of bond reduced

questions.explanation: A loose/oxidised clamp could fail under vibration or fault; C2 — clean / replace. If continuity is lost completely with the bond effectively absent, the call lifts to C1 / on-site remedy.

questions.prompt: Lighting circuit installed in 1995 with no RCD, in current dwelling. Code (typical):

options.B: C3 — improvement recommended (later editions added RCD requirement)

questions.explanation: BS 7671 not retrospective. Lighting circuit complying with the 1995 edition but not the current edition is typically C3. The improvement is to add 30 mA RCD protection.

questions.prompt: Structural steel confirmed extraneous-conductive-part, no main bonding. Code:

options.B: C2 — extraneous-part not bonded

questions.explanation: Confirmed extraneous-conductive-part requires main bonding to maintain equipotential. Absence is potentially dangerous (C2) — install bonding sized per Table 54.8.

questions.prompt: MCB swapped to wrong type (Type D where Type B was needed; Zs no longer satisfies disconnection time). Code:

options.B: C2 — disconnection time may not be met

questions.explanation: Type D requires lower Zs to disconnect within the required time. If measured Zs exceeds the Type D limit, ADS may fail; potentially dangerous, C2 — replace with the correct device or address Zs.

questions.prompt: Spur added to ring final in 1.0 mm² T+E. Code:

options.B: C2 — undersized conductor for circuit fault current

questions.explanation: 1.0 mm² T+E cannot carry a 32 A ring final's fault current safely. C2 — replace with appropriately sized cable (e.g. 2.5 mm² T+E).

questions.prompt: Old rewireable fuse board, no RCD on accessible socket-outlets in active dwelling. Code (typical):

options.B: C2 — additional protection required for sockets used by ordinary persons

questions.explanation: Current consensus is C2 for missing RCD additional protection on accessible sockets in active dwellings. Some inspectors apply C3 to plainly historic untouched installations; the trend is toward C2.

questions.prompt: Polarity reversed at one socket (single socket only). Code:

options.B: C2 — switching is now in the neutral conductor

questions.explanation: Reversed polarity at a single socket means single-pole switching breaks the neutral, leaving line connected. Potentially dangerous (C2). Some inspectors lift to C1 if foreseeable shock risk is high.

questions.prompt: 32 A MCB on 4 mm² T+E run in insulation (Iz ~27 A under method 100). Code:

options.B: C2 — overload protection not coordinated

questions.explanation: Cable Iz < device In means overload protection cannot be guaranteed; C2 — redesign protection or reduce load to match cable rating.

questions.prompt: Class I luminaire with no CPC connected, body within reach in a domestic kitchen. Code:

options.B: C2 — fault protection not satisfied
options.C: C1 — likely where reachable Class I metalwork could become live under fault
options.D: Either B or C depending on accessibility

questions.explanation: BPG4 invites judgement: reachable Class I metalwork without a CPC is often C1; less accessible / low-risk metalwork can be C2. Document the use case and code accordingly.

questions.prompt: Recently extended kitchen with new dishwasher socket, no RCD additional protection. Code:

options.B: C2 — current edition requires RCD on accessible socket-outlets

questions.explanation: Modern installation work must comply with the current edition. A new socket-outlet without RCD protection is C2; remedy by adding 30 mA RCD or RCBO protection promptly.

questions.prompt: Sheath stripped too far back inside an enclosure, basic insulation intact. Code:

options.B: C2 — mechanical protection reduced, foreseeable progression

questions.explanation: Inside an enclosure, missing sheath reduces mechanical protection. Re-make the termination so adequate sheath enters the enclosure. C2 typical; C1 if basic insulation already breached.

questions.prompt: An empty MCB way in the consumer unit with the MCB still fitted but no cable connected. Code:

options.B: C2 — exposed live terminal could be inadvertently energised in maintenance
options.D: Either B or C depending on accessibility

questions.explanation: Currently exposed live terminal = C1 (basic protection); covered now but a foreseeable maintenance event would expose it = C2. Remedy is to remove the MCB and blank the way.

questions.prompt: Earthing conductor undersized at MET (10 mm² for 100 A PME, BS 7671 minimum 16 mm²). Code:

options.B: C2 — earthing conductor inadequate for PME fault current

questions.explanation: PME earthing conductors must be sized to handle combined neutral / earth fault currents. Under-sized conductor is potentially dangerous (C2) — upgrade to BS 7671 Table 54.7 sizing.

questions.prompt: Active arcing inside a distribution board cover. Code:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Active arcing is an immediate danger; isolate the affected board, label, notify duty holder same day. C1 — Unsatisfactory.

questions.prompt: Burnt-out neutral termination at a busbar, contained, cooled, no exposed live parts. Code:

options.B: C2 — repair / rebuild promptly
options.C: C1 if active heat or exposed live parts
options.D: Either B or C depending on observed condition

questions.explanation: BPG4 calls for judgement. Cooled, contained burn damage is C2 with prompt remedy; active arcing or exposed live parts is C1 with on-site make-safe.

questions.prompt: RCD failure on a circuit feeding several outdoor sockets. Code:

options.B: C2 — additional protection impaired
options.C: C1 — likely if the RCD is the sole protective measure on accessible outdoor sockets
options.D: Either B or C depending on whether other protective measures are intact

questions.explanation: Outdoor socket use depends on RCD additional protection. Where the RCD is the sole guarantor against direct contact, failure lifts to C1. Where ADS still works robustly, C2 with prompt replacement.

questions.prompt: Older red/black colour code wiring, used in installation that has not been altered. Code:

options.B: C3
options.C: Satisfactory — old colours are not in themselves a defect

questions.explanation: Old colours alone are compliant for their era. Where new and old wiring meet, identification is essential — typically a C2 or C3 depending on the situation. The colour itself is not a defect.

questions.prompt: BS 3036 fuse on a 5 A lighting circuit, otherwise sound, ADS times still met. Code:

options.B: C2
options.C: C3 (or Satisfactory if ADS times comfortably met)

questions.explanation: BPG4: a BS 3036 fuse with ADS times verified and the rest of the protective measures intact is typically Satisfactory or C3 (improvement recommended). Failure to meet disconnection times lifts to C2.

questions.prompt: Fire damage on a circuit's accessory and cable, contained, cooled, no exposed live parts. Code:

options.B: C2 — replace damaged components, re-test
options.C: C1 if continuing fire risk or exposed live parts
options.D: Either B or C depending on the inspector's assessment

questions.explanation: Contained, cooled damage with no exposed live parts is C2 with prompt remedy. Active heat / smoke / exposed live parts is C1 with on-site make-safe.

questions.prompt: Damaged armoured cable gland with steel armour exposed, cores intact. Code:

options.B: C2 (likely) — mechanical / earthing reliability of SWA reduced
options.C: C1 if the cores are damaged exposing live parts
options.D: Either B or C depending on observed condition

questions.explanation: BPG4 again: damaged gland with intact cores is C2; damaged gland with breached basic insulation and exposed live parts is C1. The inspector documents the actual condition.

questions.prompt: Retail unit with no RCD additional protection on customer-facing socket-outlets. Code:

options.B: C2 — additional protection required for accessible sockets in commercial premises used by ordinary persons

questions.explanation: Commercial premises with public access fall under the requirement for RCD additional protection on accessible sockets. Absence is C2.

questions.prompt: Missing previous EIC / Schedule of Test Results held by duty holder. Code (typical):

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Missing certification is a documentation issue, not a present danger. C3 — the duty holder should retain certification going forward; the inspector still produces the EICR based on current condition.

questions.prompt: Visible discolouration / heat damage at a circuit termination, with active burning smell. Code:

options.B: C2

questions.explanation: Active burning smell + discolouration is an active fault. Isolate the circuit and label it, notify the duty holder same day, and code C1 with a clear description.

questions.prompt: Cable tray (metal) used to support insulated cables, not connected to protective earth. Code:

options.B: C2 — exposed-conductive-part / extraneous-part not earthed

questions.explanation: Metal containment that could become live under fault is treated as exposed-conductive-part and must be earthed. Absence of earthing is C2 — install dedicated CPC or bond to MET.

questions.prompt: Loose earth pin contact at an accessible socket-outlet. Code (typical):

options.B: C2 — fault protection on connected appliances impaired
options.C: C1 (likely if Class I appliance is regularly connected)
options.D: Either B or C depending on use case

questions.explanation: BPG4 invites judgement: a passively defective earth contact is C2; if the socket regularly feeds Class I appliances and is in a domestic kitchen / bathroom area, the call may lift to C1.

questions.prompt: PV system DC isolator without correct DC-rated labelling. Code:

options.B: C2 — emergency isolation could be unsafe due to incorrect identification

questions.explanation: DC isolation labelling matters for emergency response. Wrong / missing labelling is potentially dangerous (C2) — relabel and verify polarity / orientation.

questions.prompt: Tape-wrapped twisted joint at exposed loft-level cable run. Code:

options.B: C2 (typical) — joint not made in suitable terminal/enclosure, foreseeable progression
options.C: C1 if visibly hot, arcing, or with exposed live parts
options.D: Either B or C depending on observed condition

questions.explanation: BPG4 invites judgement: cool, intact, securely insulated tape joint is C2; hot or visibly arcing or with exposed live parts lifts to C1 with on-site make-safe.

questions.prompt: MET earth conductor terminated via a hand-tight cable lug, found loose. Code:

options.B: C2 — fault-protection earth path could be lost
options.C: C1 if continuity is effectively lost or live conductor exposed
options.D: Either B or C depending on continuity testing

questions.explanation: BPG4 calls for judgement: loose-but-continuous is C2; effectively open earth or exposed conductor is C1 with on-site make-safe.

questions.prompt: Sheltered-housing dwelling with fixed mobility-aid charging point, no RCD protection. Code:

options.B: C2 — additional protection required for circuits accessible to ordinary persons (especially vulnerable occupants)

questions.explanation: Vulnerable-user environments demand the protective measures expected of the current edition. Absent RCD additional protection on a fixed-equipment circuit is potentially dangerous (C2).

questions.prompt: Cooker control unit with switched 13 A socket on; non-functional shutters; live terminals not currently exposed. Code:

options.B: C2 — basic protection impaired (shutters non-functional), accessible socket
